pages.text: Independent explainer Kaspa, explained. Kaspa is proof-of-work Miners spend real computing work to make blocks. , the same mechanism as Bitcoin, but its miners don't compete for one slot in one chain. Every miner who finds a valid block keeps it, and GHOSTDAG Kaspa's live rule for ordering the blockDAG so parallel work counts. orders every honest block those miners produce into one history the whole network agrees on. Drag the slider below and watch what a single chain throws away that a blockDAG keeps. Start Here Watch a blockDAG keep what a chain would drop Block rate: i Why the range stops at 32 10 a second is Kaspa mainnet's real rate today. Bitcoin marks the low end for comparison, another network, not a Kaspa setting. 32 a second is the top of the slider because it's the fastest rate GHOSTDAG has a configured margin for: rusty-kaspa's own k table stops at 32 and panics above it. Bitcoin Kaspa mainnet Network delay: i What this number assumes Modeled with network delay fixed at 250 ms, inside a live-data bracket, not a direct Kaspa measurement of propagation. Walking 1,399 consecutive selected-parent chain blocks through api.kaspa.org (10,719 blocks, 24 August 2026) found a single-chain-equivalent delay between roughly 204 ms and 666 ms; 250 ms sits inside that bracket. The full demo's slider tops out at 5 s, rusty-kaspa's own one-way NETWORK_DELAY_BOUND worst case, a protocol constant, not a typical delay. The share is a running sample that drifts toward the modeled figure as more blocks accumulate, not a fixed reading. Both panels run at the rate above. Single chain is a model of what a longest-chain rule would lose at that rate, not Bitcoin today. Losing that fight also makes a single chain less secure as the rate climbs. pages.title: Crypto From Scratch | Kaspa Explained
pages.h1: What crypto does, and what it's worth
pages.description: What crypto is good for, what it is bad at, and why a coin has a price at all. Start from the beginning.
pages.text: Crypto from scratch What crypto does, and what it's worth Crypto earns its cost when strangers need one shared record of who owns what, and no single firm, bank, or state is trusted to keep it. Every other question, including price, comes back to that one job. The primitive A blockchain is a costly shared ledger Where that agreement is real, crypto does work nothing cheaper does. Where it isn't, a blockchain is a slow, costly database. NIST's definition, and why it's narrower than the marketing one NIST IR 8202 defines a blockchain by four properties: hard to alter, tamper-evident, replicated across many holders, and typically leaderless. Nothing in that definition requires a token, a mining reward, or decentralization beyond copy count. Bitcoin, stablecoins, NFTs, DeFi, and smart contracts are all apps layered on that one narrow structure, not defined by it. Each era is a fix for the one before it Eight eras, from pre-Bitcoin to rollups, each with its fix and mechanism Era Fix Mechanism Before Bitcoin Digital cash Faked the scarcity atoms have free. Bitcoin Double-spending PoW made rewriting payment history too costly to bother. Early mining Security market CPUs became ASICs, solo miners became warehouse farms. Litecoin and forks Parameter experiments Forked Bitcoin's code to change block time, algorithm, or scale. Ethereum Programmability A ledger that runs code, not just balances. 2017 ICOs and scaling war Fundraising outran products; Bitcoin split over how to scale. DeFi and stablecoins On-chain finance Dollar tokens and market makers turned demos into habit. Rollups and fast L1s Scale and UX Execution moved off the base chain into L2s and new L1s. Crypto has no company update lever: each side picks up new rules on its own, and a fork is what happens when they stop agreeing. Soft forks vs. hard forks, and five chains' bets Soft-fork changes tighten the rules, so upgraded nodes enforce new limits while un-upgraded nodes still see those blocks as valid. Hard-fork changes break what old software accepts, sometimes planned and boring, sometimes the moment a chain splits in two. Bitcoin Cash split over block size. Ethereum traded Bitcoin's spare rule set for programmable state. Solana-style chains bought speed with hardware most people can't run, Monero and Zcash bought privacy with heavier math and legal heat, and stablecoins bet on an issuer or a collateral pool over a central bank. Kaspa kept PoW and UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. and swapped the single chain for a blockDAG. Kaspa's fair launch is what was left after DAGLabs and several hardware, presale, and business-model paths fell through; the origin page has the sourced version. Where crypto fits Where it wins, and where it loses Four places it does real work Bearer digital assets Whoever holds the private key controls the asset; an exchange freeze cannot touch a self-held coin. Cross-border settlement Stablecoins are flawed dollar tokens, still one of crypto's clearest wins: paid abroad in minutes, not days. Programmable escrow Smart contracts hold up when the test is plain: both sides signed, a vesting date arrived. Open-network incentives Tokens pay the validators and storage hosts an open network runs on, with no one firm hiring all of them. Four places it usually loses Payments at home Cards, Pix, UPI, SEPA, and Apple Pay beat crypto on refunds, fraud handling, and support. Ordinary databases If one owner already controls the users, data, and rules, a blockchain only adds cost to a solved problem. Anything a court settles Fraud, a wrong-address payment, a divorce, a stolen name: cases courts exist for, and code cannot reach them. Facts from the physical world A blockchain keeps whatever gets typed into it. Lie about where the tuna came from and the chain keeps the lie forever. "Trustless" is the wrong word. Crypto moves trust around: what you took from the bank teller lands on code, wallets, bridges, oracles, and law. Eight tradeoffs, benefit against cost, property by property Property Benefit Cost Self-custody You hold the keys yourself Lose keys, lose funds Irreversibility Final settlement Fraud is hard to undo Public ledger Transparency and auditability Privacy leakage Permissionless access Anyone can participate Scams and junk projects thrive Programmability Automated financial logic Smart-contract and oracle risk Decentralization No single operator Slower choices and worse UX Token incentives Bootstraps open networks Price bets and rewards that misfire Global settlement Cross-border access Rules differ in every country Market value Why a coin has a price, and what the number means A token price is smoke; the question is what's burning underneath it. Four things push it: someone needs the asset to pay fees, settle a trade, stake, or post collateral; scarcity people believe in; higher rewards buying more security; and reflexivity, price rising because people expect it to. The five roles a token can play, and the beginner trap in each Role What it does Beginner warning Thing being tracked The ledger defines and transfers the asset itself. A token can exist without being useful outside speculation. Fees Users pay for scarce block space and spam resistance. Low fees help UX but can weaken fee revenue or invite spam. Security budget Miners or validators need paying to defend the record. Rewards may come from inflation, fees, or both. Collateral Some systems require staked tokens or bonded assets. Stake-based security pools around big holders and custodians. Governance Some tokens vote on parameters, treasuries, or upgrades. Governance rights can be weak, captured, or mostly symbolic. Market cap is not company value Market cap is price times circulating supply, nothing more. That much cash never had to flow in, no revenue sits behind the number, and nobody could sell the whole supply at that price. One KAS costs less than one BTC simply because there are far more of them; compare market cap and liquidity instead of unit price. Five more numbers that mislead, and what open markets help and break Price per coin means nothing without supply attached, circulating supply can differ sharply from total supply, and a low float inflates paper valuations without matching real capital. Volume can mean liquidity, hype, wash trading, or panic. Fully diluted value shows the dilution still coming, and social dominance measures attention, not uptake. Markets help: miners and validators can sell rewards, apps can price collateral, and anyone can enter or exit without asking one issuer. Markets break: pump-and-dumps run easy, insiders use retail liquidity as exit liquidity, and leverage forces violent selling. Early buyers profiting in an open market does not make an asset a Ponzi. What does: a fixed promised return, yield paid from new deposits instead of income, or hidden insiders. Initial ownership shapes trust A fair launch removes the official allocation table, not the funding and early-miner questions a premine would have paid for. Kaspa mined its supply from zero: see that shape plotted against three chains that started with a premine or a sale . Five launch models, what each buys and risks Launch model What it improves What it risks Fair launch / mined launch Lower official insider-allocation risk. No built-in treasury, early-miner advantage, harder funding. Premine Funds development, legal work, grants, audits, and integrations. Insider control, sell pressure, trust problems. Public sale or ICO Fast fundraising and broad early buyer base. Legal risk, hype buying, sloppy product work. VC allocation Real funding and business support. Unlock overhang and retail exit-liquidity risk. Airdrop Rewards users and spreads supply wider. Farming, sybil attacks, instant sell pressure. Rule: a price pump doesn't prove uptake, and a high market cap doesn't prove usefulness. A solid project can still be overpriced. Decision rule Crypto makes sense when at least three are true Fewer than three, and the project is bolting crypto onto a problem that never needed it. The hardest check: if the job is proving an off-chain fact is true, no ledger can do that for you. Shared ledger across parties that do not fully trust each other Users need to verify the rules themselves Assets must move globally, 24/7 Users need self-custody Users need censorship resistance The asset is digital or legally represented digitally Settlement speed is worth limited reversibility The product needs composability with on-chain systems A token is necessary to coordinate incentives Bridge to Kaspa Judge Kaspa where shared records need neutrality Kaspa's lane is narrow: proof of work, self-custody, global settlement, censorship resistance, fast confirmations, and later, apps that prove their own rules. A blockDAG orders parallel blocks instead of making them race for one slot. The UTXO model settles who owns what. Mass rules price the compute and storage a transaction actually costs, instead of just its byte size. Covenants let a coin carry rules about how it can be spent next. Those four mechanisms are Kaspa's answers to ordering, double-spends, state cost, and finality. Continue to the Kaspa design case Source notes Sources for the reality check Seven primary sources, with what each backs NIST IR 8202 for the definition of a blockchain. World Bank Remittance Prices Worldwide for the cost of sending money home. Chainalysis 2024 Latin America report for stablecoin use in Argentina and Brazil. IMF Understanding Stablecoins for stablecoin policy risks. BIS Annual Economic Report 2025, Chapter III on tokenized money and the systems behind it. Securitize / PR Newswire on BUIDL surpassing $1B AUM , a dated mark for tokenized funds. BIS Annual Economic Report 2022, Chapter III for the case against crypto as a money system. Next step Fill in whatever is still fuzzy Records, keys, blocks, consensus, and market cap get built up in order on the zero-start guide. pages.title: What Is Kaspa? Proof-of-Work blockDAG Explained | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: What is Kaspa? KAS, Proof of Work, blockDAGs, GHOSTDAG, 10 BPS, and what's live on mainnet versus still roadmap.
pages.text: Beginner answer What is Kaspa? Kaspa is a live proof-of-work blockDAG network. Its native coin is KAS. The network keeps Bitcoin-style mining and UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. ownership, and GHOSTDAG orders parallel blocks into one payment history. Limits get their own page: Risks and Open Questions covers adoption, node load, and security budget. The core move Parallel blocks are the whole design A block takes time to reach the rest of the world. When blocks outrun that propagation, miners build on stale information and produce competing blocks a single chain can only keep one of. Bitcoin's answer is to make blocks rare, roughly one every ten minutes, so collisions stay rare too. Why rare blocks are the fix, and what it costs At a ten-minute interval, propagation delay is small next to the interval itself, so most blocks finish spreading before the next one is found, and a collision is a rare accident rather than routine. Bitcoin never needed a rule for keeping both sides of one: discarding the loser is cheap enough. The cost lands on confirmation time instead. A payment needs several block intervals to be safe, which is why it settles at the pace it does, not in seconds. How fast blocks are found: i Why the range stops at 32 32 a second is the top of this slider because it's the fastest rate GHOSTDAG has a configured margin for: rusty-kaspa's own k table stops at 32 and panics above it. Bitcoin, 1 every 10 min Kaspa mainnet, 10/s 32/s How long a block takes to reach other miners: Opens at Kaspa's real rate, 10 blocks a second, with propagation modeled at 250 ms, inside a live-data bracket, not a Kaspa measurement of propagation itself. The slider's top end, 5 seconds, is NETWORK_DELAY_BOUND , rusty-kaspa's own one-way worst-case delay assumption, a protocol constant, not a typical delay. i Why 250 ms Walking 1,399 consecutive selected-parent chain blocks through api.kaspa.org (10,719 blocks, a 948.6 second window, 24 August 2026) found 86.9% were concurrent blocks a strict one-winner chain would have discarded, though GHOSTDAG kept nearly all of them blue. Inverting that share on this page's model gives a single-chain-equivalent delay between roughly 204 ms and 666 ms, depending on which form of the formula is solved. 250 ms sits inside that bracket. It brackets the number; it does not settle it, since a DAG's parallelism inflates the discard share past what a true single chain would show. A stricter read: on that same walk, only 2 of 10,719 blocks were ever marked red on mainnet, because k, the anticone tolerance, absorbs ordinary collisions before they turn red. That figure measures k doing its job, not propagation speed, so it is not used to set this slider. i What this model is and how it was checked A Poisson single-chain race model, not an observation of any running network. Checked against real data: Decker & Wattenhofer measured Bitcoin's stale rate at 1.69%, with a mean propagation delay of 12.6 s. Solving this model backward for that stale rate gives about 10.3 s, the same order of magnitude as the measured figure, within roughly 1.5 to 2x. Not an exact match. Both panels run at the rate above. Single chain is a model of what a longest-chain rule would lose at that rate, not a picture of Bitcoin today. Splitting hash power that way also makes a single chain less secure as the rate climbs, the DAGKNIGHT paper's own reason a longest-chain rule stops scaling. Single chain so far: 0 kept, 0 thrown away kept thrown away BlockDAG every block kept every block kept, ordered by parents Step one block How this works, and the sources Blocks arrive at random, like raindrops: a Poisson process with rate λ. A block collides with the one before it if the next block is found before the first one finishes spreading across the network, which takes time d. That gives a plain formula for how often a given block collides with at least one other: p = 1 − e −λd (λ = block rate, d = propagation delay) That collision probability is not the number this page leads with. Once a single chain keeps a block, it will not accept anything that arrives before that block finishes propagating, so a run of colliding blocks only ever keeps the first and discards the rest, the same way a non-paralyzable dead-time counter drops any event landing inside its recovery window without extending that window. Working through that identity gives a lower share than p: discarded share = λd ÷ (1 + λd) kept share = 1 ÷ (1 + λd) Inferred from the dead-time-counter identity above, matching this simulator's own discard rule rather than quoted from a source. At Kaspa's defaults (10 blocks a second, 250 ms modeled propagation), λd = 2.51, so p works out to about 92% while the discarded share is about 72%, which is the figure the running tally above converges toward. A single chain can only keep one block per collision, so the loser's work is wasted. A blockDAG references every block a miner could see when it started working, so both survive and get ordered instead of discarded. Where this comes from. Block creation as a Poisson process of rate λ, and network propagation delay as the thing that causes concurrent blocks, are exactly the model in Sompolinsky, Wyborski and Zohar's PHANTOM/GHOSTDAG paper ( eprint.iacr.org/2018/104 ): "Block creation follows a Poisson process with parameter λ," bounded by a network delay diameter D. Verified against that primary source. The paper's own math goes further than this demo: it bounds how many blocks can be created within a delay window (the anticone size k, used to tune GHOSTDAG itself), via a Poisson-tail formula in D·λ. This page's p = 1 − e −λd is the simpler building block underneath that: the chance at least one more block arrives before the first one finishes propagating, which is standard Poisson-process math (P(0 arrivals in time d) = e −λd ) and matches the same collision mechanism used in the Bitcoin fork-rate literature (Decker & Wattenhofer, Information Propagation in the Bitcoin Network , IEEE P2P 2013). Inferred from that Poisson identity rather than quoted directly from either paper. This demo simplifies further by testing only whether a block collides with the immediately preceding one, not the full multi-block anticone GHOSTDAG actually resolves; it is a simplification of the source math, not the source math itself. Playback speed scales with the rate instead of landing every setting at the same pace, on a log-compressed mapping with one fixed point: at 1 block a second, the display shows a block a second, real time. Below that point the display rate is the real rate's seventh root, compressed hard enough that a real Bitcoin block, on average one every 10 minutes, plays back roughly every 2.5 seconds here, about 240x real time, so the wait still feels slow rather than reading as a label. At 1 block a second and above there is no compression at all: Kaspa mainnet's real rate, 10 a second, plays back at 10 a second, real time, and the slider's ceiling, 32 a second, plays back at 32 a second, real time. That ceiling is not arbitrary: rusty-kaspa's k table, the anticone-size bound GHOSTDAG's own consensus code uses, runs from k = 18 at 1 block a second up to k = 362 at 32, and the code panics above 32 with "see gen_ghostdag_table for currently supported values." 32 a second is the fastest rate GHOSTDAG has a configured margin for at all. The collision math above always uses the real rate and delay, not the playback speed; only what you see on screen below 1 block a second is sped up for legibility. Respects reduced-motion: becomes a step button instead of steady motion. Kaspa keeps the fast blocks and fixes the order instead. A block points at every tip its miner could see, so two blocks found a moment apart both land in the record as parents of whatever gets mined next, exactly what the demo above just showed surviving instead of getting thrown away. The word blockDAG names that shape. GHOSTDAG reads the resulting graph and derives the order. Kaspa's origin story covers how that research reached mainnet. What you feel above is inclusion speed: mainnet makes ten blocks a second, so a broadcast transaction usually lands in a block within about a second. Inclusion is not settlement; the gap between them is what confirmations measure. Supply itself is capped on a fixed emission schedule with no premine. The ordering rule How GHOSTDAG turns a graph into one line Parents Every block names the tips its miner could see when it started hashing. Those references are the whole data structure. Coloring The k cap below decides color. Blocks that stay inside it join the blue set GHOSTDAG marks well-connected blocks blue and less-compatible ones red, for ordering and security accounting. ; the rest are marked red and keep their place, their parents, and their transactions. Spine Each block picks the parent carrying the most blue work Accumulated proof-of-work weight carried by blue blocks. It's how Kaspa compares competing DAG histories. as its selected parent The parent block that defines the main ordering path through the DAG. Not the same thing as Bitcoin's longest chain. . Chain those picks together and you get the closest thing Kaspa has to Bitcoin's longest chain. One order Walk that spine from genesis to the current tip, absorbing each mergeset The set of past blocks a new block pulls into view: how parallel work gets folded into the ordering. in turn with blue blocks ahead of red ones, and every block in the graph ends up in a single line. Miners don't take turns: independent miners publish blocks whenever they find them, so more than one can arrive at once. Advance time and watch how many arrive together, and how many get locked out. How many arrive at once varies every round. Advance time Force a count instead: − 2 blocks + Mine this many Reset Advanced: hide blocks, then release them Publish nothing for a while and mine on your own, then bring your blocks back. The rest of the network doesn't wait for you. See what happens when it already moved on without you. Hide blocks Mine a secret block Release 0 Your blocks are hidden. No one else can see or build on them yet. The rest of the network is not waiting: it keeps mining and publishing while you stay hidden. Advanced: how forgiving the network is Every block can have some other blocks beside it that it never saw. This caps how many of those are still allowed to count. Lower it, and blocks get locked out sooner. Raise it, and more blocks keep counting even when a lot of them arrive at once. Uncounted neighbors allowed (k): 3 The DAG Scroll to see more → counted in the order locked out Hover or tap any block to see why. Show what the network sees right now Linear order The one ordering every node agrees on: walk the main chain, and slot each block's counted neighbors in before its locked-out ones. How the colors get decided Every block names the tips its miner could see when it was made; those references are the whole data structure. A block's past is everything behind it, its future is everything built on top of it, and its anticone is everyone else: blocks that neither saw it nor were seen by it. Each block also picks the parent with the most accumulated work as its selected parent, chaining block to block into a main chain. A block counts (blue) if the number of already-counted blocks in its anticone stays under the cap, k. Over the cap, it's locked out (red) instead. The DAG has no single "now": blocks keep arriving in parallel, with no one moment everyone agrees on. Kaspa's answer is the virtual block, a conceptual block that is never mined and never sent to anyone; it exists only on each node's own machine, standing in for everything that node has seen. Its parents, the virtual parents, are simply that node's current tips. Among those tips, the one with the most already-counted blocks behind it becomes the virtual selected parent, better known as the sink. It's the same rule an ordinary block uses to pick its own selected parent, just applied one level up: to the node's whole view, not to a single mined block. A block's anticone Blocks that sit in neither a block's past nor its future. Nodes need an anticone rule to order these consistently. is everything neither behind it nor built on it. A single chain has no way to rank an anticone, so it discards one side. GHOSTDAG ranks it instead, by one behavioral tell: an honest miner publishes a block the instant it is found, and a miner building a secret history does the opposite. Why honest and hidden miners produce different anticones Within a propagation delay, everyone else sees an honest miner's block and starts referencing it, so its anticone stays small by construction. Nobody can reference blocks they were never shown, so a hidden miner's withheld blocks surface later carrying wide anticones. An attacker whose blocks land red spent real electricity that buys no weight in that history, which is why raising the block rate here doesn't hand the orphan rate the security budget. Confirmations Fast is not final 1 Seen Your wallet broadcasts the transaction and nodes pick it up. 2 Included A miner mines it into a proof-of-work block. 3 Ordered GHOSTDAG places it against the blocks mined in parallel. 4 Accepted Nodes accept it under Kaspa's consensus rules. 5 Confidence Reversal risk keeps falling as more blocks stack proof-of-work on top of it. Kaspa has no single stack to count. Your block sits in a graph, and what piles up on it is blue work: the proof-of-work carried by every later blue block whose history includes yours. Reversal risk falls as that weight builds, which is why Kaspa publishes no universal confirmation count. The confirmation risk demo plots that curve: drag its slider and watch reversal odds fall as wait time rises. What actually sets a safe wait, and how finality depth differs Undoing a payment means producing a competing set of blocks heavy enough to outweigh the one the network already accepted, and every new block referencing your transaction raises that bill. Wallets and explorers report the result as a confirmation count. At 10 BPS Blocks per second. Kaspa ran at 1 bps until the Crescendo activation, DAA score 110,165,000, and has run at 10 bps since. those references arrive quickly, so the risk curve drops steeply in the first seconds. Steeply is not vertically. Three things set the honest wait: the value at stake, hash rate now and how much it swings, and whether the payment can be undone outside the protocol. A shipping hold takes a thinner wait than handing over a good nobody can claw back. Exchanges and payment firms publish their own deposit rules, and those are the numbers a user meets. Finality depth The threshold past which old history counts as settled. is a different, deeper question: how far back the protocol will let anyone rewrite. It sits far past any payment wait, and once history is buried past it nodes reject a reorganization outright, which is also what makes pruning safe. Does pruning make Kaspa private? No. Pruning and missing explorer history are not privacy guarantees. UTXO state remains the consensus object, and a broadcast transaction can still be observed or archived by others before a node prunes it. Throughput Ask "TPS of what?" Status checked August 22, 2026: Kaspa mainnet runs the Crescendo The May 2025 upgrade that sped Kaspa's mainnet from one block a second to ten. -era 10 BPS network. Toccata The mainnet upgrade activated 30 June 2026 that let a coin carry enforceable spending rules, called covenants, instead of just moving from one address to another. went live at DAA 474,165,565 and changed proof and covenant capacity. Plain payment TPS tracks the 10 BPS network and transaction mix. Four workload types, and why the TPS number moves Workload Answer Why the number changes Simple L1 payments Roughly 2.5k to 3.4k TPS for plain transfers. Set by 10 BPS and block-mass limits against simple transaction mass. Covenant or programmable L1 transactions Job by job, usually below simple-payment TPS. Covenants add script work, state rules, covenant IDs, extra outputs, and storage effects. ZK Zero-knowledge: a proof that a statement is true without revealing the data behind it, so a script can accept a claim about work done elsewhere without seeing that work. proof or settlement transactions Fewer, heavier L1 transactions. One proof or settlement transaction can carry many off-chain app actions. Set by the proof system, proof size, check cost, batch size, proving time, and settlement design. Effective ZK app or future vProg throughput App by app, and it can beat raw L1 transaction TPS. Count app actions per proof batch or settlement cycle. State access and prover work are the real limits. None of that makes throughput unlimited. A proof proves a statement about chosen inputs, so outside facts still need an anchor: a light client, finality certificate, reporter set, oracle, or challenge process. Build a transaction and see which mass dimension gets charged Every transaction takes up room in a block. Kaspa counts that room as mass Kaspa's own unit for how much block space a transaction uses. Not bytes, not KAS: the network charges a transaction for whichever kind of work costs it most, and only that one. , not bytes. Build one below and see how many transactions like it fit in a block. Plain 1-in 1-out payment 1-in 2-out with change Covenant transaction ZK proof transaction Reset Build the transaction Inputs 1 Outputs 1 Amount per output (KAS) 1,000 Payload / proof bytes 0 Advanced: script per input Simple signature (1 signature check) Covenant / compute budget Compute budget units per input 50 How many fit in a block 0 transactions like this fit in a block 0 TPS at 10 blocks a second, if every block were full of this shape. Advanced: which limit is binding A transaction is charged for the largest of three costs, never the sum: compute (running its script), storage (new state it creates), and transient (proof data). Whichever is largest decides how many fit. Compute mass · binding i What counts as compute mass Cost of running this transaction's signature and script checks. 0 / 500,000 mass units Storage mass · binding i What counts as storage mass Cost of new state this transaction leaves behind, such as a change output. 0 / 500,000 mass units Transient mass · binding i What counts as transient mass Cost of proof data attached to the transaction, cleared after the block that included it. 0 / 1,000,000 mass units Show the mass formulas Transaction size size = 94 (fixed header: version, in/out counts, locktime, subnetwork id, gas, payload hash, payload length) + payload_bytes + inputs × (118 fixed bytes: outpoint 36, sig-script length field 8, signature script ~66, sequence 8; +2 if covenant/v1) + outputs × (52 fixed bytes (value 8, version 2, script-length field 8, P2PK-style script 34) + 34 per output, if that output carries a covenant id) Compute mass compute_mass = size × mass_per_tx_byte (1) + Σ(2 + output_script_len) × mass_per_script_pub_key_byte (10) + script_mass script_mass = inputs × 1 sigop × GRAMS_PER_SIGOP_COUNT_UNIT (1000) [simple] = inputs × compute_budget_units × GRAMS_PER_COMPUTE_BUDGET_UNIT (100) [covenant] Transient mass transient_mass = size × TRANSIENT_BYTE_TO_MASS_FACTOR (4) Storage mass ( KIP Kaspa Improvement Proposal: the process that specifies, reviews, and merges a protocol change. Nothing on this site counts as shipped without a merged KIP and a release tag. -0009) C = STORAGE_MASS_PARAMETER (1,000,000,000,000) utxo_plurality(output) = ceil((63 + script_bytes + 32 if covenant else 0) / 100) A P2PK-style output (script 34) has plurality 1. A covenant-carrying output (63 + 34 + 32 = 129 bytes) crosses the 100-byte unit and has plurality 2, which squares its weight below. storage_mass = max(0, outputs × plurality² × C / out_amount_sompi − inputs × C / in_amount_sompi) in_amount_sompi assumes no fee: total out value split evenly across inputs. Which dimension binds Compute and storage share a 500,000 block-mass limit; transient's limit is 1,000,000, so it is normalized to the same scale before comparison: transient_norm = transient_mass × 500,000/1,000,000. tx_mass = max(compute_mass, storage_mass, transient_norm) tx_per_block = floor(500,000 / tx_mass) TPS = tx_per_block × 10 blocks/second This models a standard Schnorr P2PK-style input/output shape and assumes value is conserved with no fee. Real network TPS is lower once relay policy, fee markets, and mempool behavior are added on top of this pure mass ceiling. Formulas verified against rusty-kaspa mass code , consensus params , and core constants . Offline calculator, no network requests. Where the payment numbers come from Kaspa mainnet makes ten blocks per second. Current mainnet params cap compute and storage block mass at 500,000, which gives a budget of 5,000,000 transaction mass per second before policy, fees, relay, storage shape, and real mempool behavior come in. A signed plain P2PK-style 1-input, 1-output payment costs roughly 1.6k mass by the code's careful math; add a change output and a 1-input, 2-output payment runs closer to 2.0k mass. Divide the block budget by those shapes and the count lands around 250 to 300 simple transactions per block, the mid-2k to low-3k TPS lane at 10 BPS. Leaner shapes and rounding push the top end to the often-quoted 3.4k TPS. Benchmarks built on fake minimum-size transactions score higher than that, and what they measure is a lab ceiling. A raw count of transactions per block hides the real limit, which is mass. The implementation measures three dimensions: compute mass from serialized bytes, script-public-key bytes, and signature-operation or compute-budget work; transient byte mass; and storage mass. Each is normalized against its own block limit, and a transaction is charged whichever of the three is largest, never their sum. Anything that makes a transaction bigger, from extra outputs to covenant metadata to proof bytes, crowds out the simple transfers competing for the same budget. Kaspa's docs put the payload ceiling around 25 KB when payload data dominates a standard transaction, because the standard transaction mass ceiling and transient byte accounting still apply on top of it. Toccata leaves the payment limit alone. Transient mass rises from 500,000 to 1,000,000 at activation, while the compute and storage reference limit holds at 500,000, and the Toccata guide ties that rise to fitting STARK-sized proofs. Toccata also adds v1 transaction fields such as output covenant data and input compute commitments, and raises the standard minimum relay fee. It is mostly an upgrade to what L1 transactions can say and check. Piece What it adds TPS implication KIP-17 covenants Transaction introspection and script tools for stateful UTXO rules. More expressive transactions run heavier than simple payments. KIP-20 covenant IDs A 32-byte covenant identifier that gives covenant state a lineage. Backs asset rules, at the cost of extra data and checking work. KIP-16 ZK precompile OpZkPrecompile for proof paths such as Groth16 and RISC0-Succinct. Proof transactions spend L1 room on checking work. Little of that room goes to moving coins. KIP-21 sequencing commitments Partitioned lane commitments. Cuts app proving cost. It is not itself an end-user TPS number. vProgs remain roadmap architecture. Toccata ships the parts vProg-style systems need without shipping vProgs. KIP-21 stops every prover from having to follow the whole DAG for every app: its partitioned commitment design targets O(activity) proving, so a prover for one app lane tracks only that lane. Current params cap user-lane churn at 50 non-coinbase lanes per block and 1,000,000,000 gas per lane, which at 10 BPS is a worst-case 500 user-lane updates per second, and user transaction throughput still needs its own transaction-shape math on top. The public kaspanet/vprogs repo shows where the build is headed. Michael Sutton A core Kaspa developer who led the Rust rewrite and much of 2026's covenant and scripting work, including Argent and Silverscript. 's Argent is an actor-based language and compiler that already builds multi-contract covenant apps into Silverscript A higher-level language that compiles down to Kaspa script, so a covenant can be written as readable rules instead of hand-assembled opcodes. , with an audit as the gate its README sets before real use. Covenants A coin that can carry its own rule Since Toccata went live at DAA score 474,165,565, a Kaspa coin can carry a rule about how it may move next. The network checks that rule the same way it checks a signature: a vault can ask for a delay and a backup key, an escrow a release or a refund. What Toccata turned on, KIP by KIP KIP-17 A UTXO can read the transaction spending it and require a matching next output: vaults, escrow, spend caps, refunds. KIP-20 Covenant IDs give covenant state a lineage consensus tracks, blocking fake lookalikes. KIP-16 A script checks a proof from a chosen proof system, initially Groth16 and RISC0-Succinct, instead of L1 running every app step itself. KIP-21 Sequencing commitments let an app prove its own lane instead of almost the whole DAG. vProgs Not part of what activated. Full vProgs, for shared app state many users mutate at once, are still roadmap architecture. See status . Based apps Apps anchor state to Kaspa ordering and settle proofs back to it, with no separate sequencer. No virtual machine, no accounts, no global shared state. App logic lives in bounded UTXO steps or proofs. A live demo that tries to break a covenant vault is on build on Kaspa . Primary sources: KIP-17 , KIP-20 , KIP-16 , KIP-21 , and Michael Sutton's Toccata hard-fork outlook . Live vs next What's live, what's not Six claims checked against mainnet Claim Status Safer wording Kaspa is Proof of Work, 10 BPS, ordered by GHOSTDAG Live All three describe current mainnet in the Crescendo era. Toccata has activated on mainnet Activated Toccata crossed its mainnet activation score. That protocol switch is live; app, wallet, explorer, and SDK support still need their own checks. July 2026 is a sudden emission cliff Misleading Emission steps down once a month, keyed to DAA score. The calendar has nothing to do with it. July 2026 sits inside one of those scheduled steps. GHOSTDAG is DAGKnight, or DAGKnight is current mainnet consensus Research DAGKnight is a separate, later consensus design, still research and implementation work. Current mainnet consensus runs GHOSTDAG. 10 BPS means payments are final immediately No 10 BPS is live and speeds up inclusion. Reversal risk falls as proof-of-work stacks up, so a recipient waits for the depth the amount at stake deserves. The blockDAG means unlimited TPS No Throughput is bounded by block capacity, mempool policy, fees, and demand. Anything not listed here goes through the claim fact-check , which sorts a claim into live, testnet, targeted, roadmap, research, wrong, unsupported, or out of scope. Sources Check it yourself Kaspa Research carries the protocol lineage; Rusty Kaspa is the code that runs it, including k and the rest of the consensus parameters. Kaspa.com's Learn Kaspa has term-by-term references for anticone, mergeset, and blue work: vocabulary and mechanics, not protocol status. Kaspa.com Learn Kaspa article index (50 articles) Scaling Problem Pruning Depth KIP 10 Learning Guide KIP 20 KIP 21 OpCodes Block Anatomy DAGKNIGHT Smart Contracts Storage Mass Block Processing Median Time Timestamp Validation Virtual Parents TX Validation Coinbase Transactions Sink Selection DAA Score Transaction Mass Virtual Block Anticone Finalization BPS Mergeset Limit Cheat Sheet Merge Depth DAA Window Finality Depth What is Kaspa k-Cluster Selection Intro Blue Score/Work First-Order Pruning DAG Terminology GHOSTDAG Simplified Parents/Mergeset Second-Order Pruning UTXO Model MuHash Body/Header Linking BlockDAG Archival/Full Nodes Finality Types Transaction Selection K Parameter Blue Work Blue vs Red Mergeset Parent Chain Watch the network: a live read of Kaspa's own public API, not a simulation Real blocks, read live from Kaspa's own public API. Kaspa makes about 10 a second; this checks in every 9 seconds and shows what it actually fetched, not a simulation of the rest. If the API can't be reached, it says so instead of faking it. Can't reach the public network right now. Retrying every 9 seconds. The explanation below still applies; nothing on this page is invented while it waits. – blocks racing for the same spot right now. Kaspa doesn't make them wait in line. Measuring the network's real pace… Reading the first blocks… Pause Checking every 9 seconds. – of the blocks this page has watched this session carried nothing but the miner's own reward. Kaspa's own measured baseline runs the same way: about 0.9 transactions per second, and 88.3% of its raw transaction count is coinbase, one per block (site data, read from api.kaspa.org, 2026‑08‑22). Kaspa targets 10 new blocks every second. Most of what you're watching arrive is a block holding exactly one transaction: the miner paying itself. What this page shows, what it can't, and why Blocks, in parallel Kaspa doesn't pick one miner's block and discard the rest the way a single-chain network does. Several blocks can be valid at once; GHOSTDAG later orders and merges them instead of throwing them away. The count at the top of this page is tipHashes from a live read of api.kaspa.org/info/blockdag : the number of block tips the network is holding open right now. Each new tip is then fetched individually from api.kaspa.org/blocks/{blockId} . Who mined it Each block card names the payout address and the self-reported miner tag from the block's own coinbase data (the API's extra.minerAddress and extra.minerInfo fields). Neither is a verified identity: a pool can rotate payout addresses, and the tag is a plain string the miner chose to write, not something the network checks. This site's own data notes 32 distinct coinbase payout addresses over a short sample as "block producers," explicitly flagging that rotation would inflate that count. Treat every miner label here the same way. Blue and red A block tagged red below was real and mined honestly, but arrived too late in its local ordering to be counted in the ledger's accepted history; a "blue" block was. That is GHOSTDAG's actual job: keep the block, decide whether it counts. What's inside: mostly nothing yet A block with only its own coinbase transaction and zero spends is marked Empty . Most blocks arrive that way today. That is not this page failing to find activity: it is Kaspa's actual current usage, matching the sitewide figure above ( data/l1-chains.json , cross-checked against live API reads). Covenants When a transaction output carries a network-verified covenantId , this page shows a covenant tag. That field comes straight from the API's own parsed transaction data, not a guess: Toccata-era Kaspa enforces covenants and covenant IDs in consensus; see build-on-kaspa#covenant-adoption for how many are actually running. They are uncommon in the ordinary block feed; expect long stretches with none. App attribution: only where it's really written down Kaspa has no protocol-level field that names an app. What this page can honestly show is narrower: some transactions carry a plain-text tag at the front of their payload, such as ciph_msg:1:comm:… , which identifies the on-chain messaging protocol some Kaspa apps use to write encrypted messages into transactions. When a payload starts with a tag like that, this page shows an app: ciph_msg pill and nothing more: it is reading a literal string the transaction's own sender chose to include, not inferring anything. Any other payload here is unlabeled binary; guessing what wrote it would be exactly the kind of fabricated attribution this page exists not to do, so it stays unlabeled. A ZK opcode call is not shown Kaspa's script system supports a ZK verifier opcode, but the public REST API returns transaction scripts as opaque hex, not as decoded opcodes. Detecting one would mean disassembling script bytes client-side and matching a specific opcode value, which this page does not attempt. If that byte-level check turns out to be cheap and reliable, it's a reasonable thing to add later; today it isn't shown, rather than shown as a guess. What a full block explorer has that this page doesn't Explorers like Kaspa.stream run their own indexer against a database, which lets them show things a single API read cannot: a miner leaderboard built by clustering many blocks' payout addresses over time, top-address balances, and historical charts. Every one of those requires storing and aggregating history somewhere; a static page calling the public API on each visit has no database to build that from, and re-deriving it client-side on every load would mean hammering the API far past anything reasonable. This page only shows what one API read, right now, actually contains. Why this only shows a handful of blocks per check api.kaspa.org sits behind a Cloudflare edge cache with max-age=8 : two requests inside that window get the identical cached response, so checking faster than every 8 seconds would not surface a single extra block, only waste requests. This page checks every 9 seconds. But Kaspa itself is producing roughly 10 blocks a second, so each check's tipHashes array (the network's current open tip set, typically 5 to 9 hashes) is a small sample of everything that actually happened since the last check, not the full count. The line above the block feed states both numbers plainly: how many blocks the network produced in that window against how many this page could fetch and show. The blocks-per-second figure next to it is not looked up anywhere; it is computed live from the change in blockCount between this page's own polls. Endpoints used: api.kaspa.org/info/blockdag (tip hashes and blockCount , polled every 9 seconds; the API's own cache doesn't refresh faster than about 8 seconds, confirmed live 2026-08-22) and api.kaspa.org/blocks/{blockId} (one call per newly seen tip, header + transactions + color, capped at 16 per check; observed tip-set width stayed at 5-9 across dozens of live samples, and no per-IP rate limit is documented or was observed). Source for the API surface: api.kaspa.org/openapi.json . Baseline throughput and coinbase-share figures: this site's data/l1-chains.json , cross-checked against live reads on 2026-08-22. Covenant and block-producer caveats: this site's own CLAIMS.yml . Independent read of Kaspa's public API. Runs entirely in your browser; nothing is stored or sent anywhere. pages.h1: KIP Kaspa Improvement Proposal: the process that specifies, reviews, and merges a protocol change. Nothing on this site counts as shipped without a merged KIP and a release tag. s and KCCs
pages.description: A live tracker of Kaspa's change proposals. It reads the repositories direct, so it cannot go stale.
pages.text: Proposal tracker KIP Kaspa Improvement Proposal: the process that specifies, reviews, and merges a protocol change. Nothing on this site counts as shipped without a merged KIP and a release tag. s and KCCs Two separate processes decide what Kaspa becomes. One changes the protocol, one does not. A Kaspa Improvement Proposal changes consensus, node behavior, or a client API, and ships when implemented and activated. A Kaspa Call for Conventions is the opposite: an agreement between builders about how to encode a token, name a field, or shape an ABI, with no consensus change. The KCC README draws the line itself: "KCCs do not propose changes to Kaspa consensus or core-node behavior." A merged KIP marked Active is protocol law; an open KCC pull request is a draft people are still arguing about. Kaspa Improvement Proposals 15 proposals total, 11 marked Active, read live from the KIP repository and grouped below by number. Implemented means running; Active means merged and adopted; Proposed and Draft mean the argument is still open; Rejected means considered and turned down. KIP-2 proposes replacing GHOSTDAG's fixed margin with one that adapts to actual latency. Try it below. Try it: fixed margin (GHOSTDAG) versus adjustable margin (DAGKnight, KIP-2) Raising the block rate does not speed confirmation up. It slows it down. GHOSTDAG has to assume a worst-case network delay in advance, and holding that assumption fixed while blocks get faster makes the DAG KNIGHT paper's own confirmation-time bound grow without limit, the two sides below differing only in whether the delay term is that fixed assumption or the delay actually happening. Sompolinsky puts a number on it: going from 10 to 100 blocks a second would need a new k hard-forked in, and "confirmation of transactions will take tens of seconds at least, about 8x long." DAGKnight drops the assumption and tracks the delay actually happening. Push the sliders. Block rate (blocks/sec) 10 blocks/sec (Kaspa mainnet's Crescendo-era rate) rusty-kaspa ships a lookup table that stops at 32 blocks/sec. The formula behind it runs at any rate; the table is the limit, not the math. Push λ up while D stays fixed and PHANTOM's own confirmation time under attack grows exponentially in the paper's own bound, the harder reason to stop, not a shrinking security threshold: that decay is Nakamoto Consensus's problem, not PHANTOM's. Assumed worst-case latency (D) D = 5.0 s → configured margin (k) = 124 Actual latency 2.0 s (margin (k) this actually needs: 55) Healthy (0.5 s) Typical (2 s) Congested (5 s) Adversarial spike (12 s) Attacker's mining share 10% GHOSTDAG Live · fixed margin Mainnet computes this margin from a fixed table; nothing exists past 32 blocks/sec. configured margin (k) 124 margin size needed 31 confirmation bound, no visible attack (D max fixed) 12.4 s Within the cap. Anticones stay inside k; nothing looks like an attack. DAGKnight Research · adjustable margin No table to run out of: margin tracks the latency actually happening. effective margin (k) right now 55 cost: wider merge sets moderate confirmation bound, no visible attack (D t tracked) 5.5 s No cap to exceed. It operates at the size current conditions require, and relaxes again once they calm, never retuned by a person. The "confirmation bound" row above runs the DAG KNIGHT paper's own no-visible-attack formula (§1.5.2), which carries no unspecified constant: at a fixed 2 s delay it gives 12 s at 1 block/sec, 43 s at 10, and 402 s (6.7 min) at 100, a 9.3× increase that lines up with Sompolinsky's own account, "confirmation of transactions will take tens of seconds at least, about 8x long." The paper's separate, far rougher worst-case bound for a visible attack, whose constant the paper leaves unstated, sits one click down. Also see: calm versus under attack, for DAGKnight alone Research Same formula and the same three dials above (block rate, actual latency as D t , attacker's mining share), but a different comparison: not GHOSTDAG against DAGKnight, just DAGKnight's own confirmation bound in the two regimes the paper analyzes, no visible attack versus one visibly under way. No visible attack Every block looks honest right now. predicted wait Attack visibly under way An attacker is actively forking the DAG. predicted wait What this costs Not shipped, not parameter-free, efficiency unsolved. Every caveat, with sources Not shipped. Mainnet runs GHOSTDAG. KIP-2 is Status: Proposed; the dagknight branch is active, unmerged development on kaspanet's own repo, most recently "Merge branch 'dk-umc-proposed' into dagknight" on August 14, 2026. Still no testnet, no activation date. Not actually parameter-free. The paper still requires a client-set bound D, and D must cover the latency an attacker could cause, not what the network is currently showing (Pass-Shi, Theorem 14). A calm network does not license a low D. A visible attack does not slow down every payment. As long as a transaction has no visible conflicting spend, its ordering is commutative with recent transactions, so it can still confirm on the optimistic timeline above even while the pessimistic case is playing out elsewhere in the DAG (§4, footnote 14). Efficiency is unsolved. KIP-2 itself lists the current DAGKnight pseudocode as "highly inefficient" and its rewrite as unfinished work, a stated reason this is still research four years on. The 32 blocks/sec ceiling on the slider above belongs to GHOSTDAG, not to DAGKnight. rusty-kaspa's Bps<BPS>::ghostdag_k() is a hardcoded match on precomputed values for 1 through 32 blocks/sec; the fallback arm past that reads panic!("see gen_ghostdag_table for currently supported values") ( consensus/core/src/config/bps.rs , checked 2026-08-22). GHOSTDAG needs a k chosen in advance for a given rate, so running it past 32 needs a developer to compute a new k and hard-fork the network; nothing today defines one there. DAGKnight's whole premise, per KIP-2 , is removing that a priori k, so it has no table to run out of, which is why this slider lets it keep going. That range is shown to demonstrate the gap, not to assert a target: KIP-2 lists the optimal block rate as open research with no number recommended, and the widely repeated "100 blocks/sec, netsplit-resilient" figure traces only to kaspa.org's marketing pages, unconfirmed by any KIP, release, or core-contributor statement. No published cost figure exists, but the efficiency work is real and some of it now sits on kaspanet's own branch, not just a side fork. Contributor coderofstuff (40 commits to kaspanet/rusty-kaspa) develops the UMC-voting redesign on personal fork branches first, then merges it directly into kaspanet/rusty-kaspa's own dagknight branch: the dk-umc-proposed branch merged in on August 14, 2026, identical commit and all. Their explanatory write-up naming the bottleneck behind KIP-2's "highly inefficient" (the paper's recursive UMC-voting algorithm at O(n squared) worst case, with an O(n times K) amortized replacement proposed) still lives only on an unofficial personal wiki, not kaspanet's own docs. It is real, named engineering inside the project's own repository, still unmerged to master and not reviewed or adopted as the shipped algorithm. Details below. Model, formula, and citations GHOSTDAG's k comes from rusty-kaspa's own derivation, reproduced exactly for this page: k = min k̂ such that P(anticone > k̂) < δ , computed from x = 2·D·λ (D = assumed max delay in seconds, λ = blocks/second) via a Poisson-tail sum, with mainnet's constants NETWORK_DELAY_BOUND = 5s and GHOSTDAG_TAIL_DELTA = 0.01 ( consensus/core/src/config/{constants,bps}.rs ). At λ = 10 blocks/s, D = 5 s gives k = 124, matching the compiled table in bps.rs exactly (verified: 1 bps → 18, 2 → 31, 5 → 67, 10 → 124). This page's block-rate slider moves λ directly through that same formula; the D and actual-latency sliders move the two delay terms. bps 1 2 5 10 k (D = 5 s) 18 31 67 124 Does raising the block rate under GHOSTDAG lengthen confirmation? Checked against the DAG KNIGHT paper directly, not assumed. Verified, direct quote (§1.2): "many blocks are created in parallel, blocks suffer from larger anticones, and transactions take longer to confirm. This scenario represents either a slow down in the network, or a system intentionally parameterized with a high block rate, e.g., λ = 10 blocks per second," the same section adding "Kaspa's convergence time remains in the order of tens of seconds even when its latency is way below 10 seconds." Also verified, direct quote (§1.5.2): the paper's own optimistic (no visible attack) confirmation-time bound is O((ln(1/ε)/λ + D)/(1−2α) + D²λ), which grows both from the additive D term and from the D²λ term as λ rises, for fixed D. That formula, not a k/λ approximation and not the paper's separate worst-case bound, is what the "confirmation bound" readouts above compute directly: the fixed side uses D max , this widget's D slider, held fixed regardless of what the network is actually doing; the adaptive side uses D t , the actual-latency slider, tracked instead. Swapping one delay term for the other is the entire difference between the two readouts, the same PHANTOM-versus- KNIGHT split the paper draws in Table 1 below. ε is fixed at 0.01 (1% error tolerance, stated on the widget) rather than exposed as a fifth slider, and the shared attacker-share slider above supplies α to both sides. Unlike the paper's pessimistic (visible-attack) bound one click down, this formula carries no unspecified constant, so every digit it prints is a real number the paper commits to, not an illustrative placeholder, and it never needs log-space formatting to avoid overflow. Sompolinsky's "about 8x" figure, reproduced twice, neither time by inventing a constant. Bitcoin Takeover, S17 E36 (31:06), on moving from 10 to 100 blocks a second under GHOSTDAG: "you will need to hardcode in the hard fork a change of the parameter K in the network in the consensus, which would imply that confirmation of transactions will take tens of seconds at least, about 8x long." Both halves of that sentence come straight out of the optimistic formula above: at a fixed 2 s delay it gives 43 s at 10 blocks/sec, his "tens of seconds," and 402 s (6.7 min) at 100, a 9.3× increase, his "about 8x," with no constant chosen to make it land, stated on screen next to the widget above. A second, independent check gives a close second number: the margin formula, fully verified against rusty-kaspa's own bps.rs table and also carrying no unspecified constant, has the required margin k climb from 124 blocks at 10 bps to 1,074 blocks at 100 bps holding D fixed at 5 s, an 8.66× increase. The reading behind that second check: 10× more blocks per second would buy 10× faster confirmation only if the margin could stay fixed; because GHOSTDAG's own security proof forces k to grow with λ at fixed D, the actual speedup is far smaller, which is what "about 8x" is describing. The paper's separate worst-case (visible-attack) bound, one click down, tells the same directional story, unbounded growth in λ at fixed D, but its constant c is left unspecified by the paper (§1.5.2), so it cannot be tuned to hit a specific multiple without inventing a value this page has no basis for, and neither of the two checks above uses it. Table 1, transcribed. The paper directly compares four ordering rules' asymptotic convergence time, in blocks (multiply by λ⁻¹ for seconds, per the paper's own note under the table). D max is an a priori worst-case latency bound fixed in advance; D t is a bound on the current, recent latency. Protocol Visible attack No visible attack Nakamoto Consensus O((ln(1/ε) + D t λ) / max{0, (1−α)/(1+D t λ) − α}) same, asymptotically PHANTOM O(exp(c₁·D max λ/(1−2α)) + ln(1/ε)/(1−2α)) O((ln(1/ε) + D max λ)/(1−2α)) SPECTRE does not converge O((ln(1/ε) + D t λ)/(1−2α)) KNIGHT O(exp(c₂·D t λ/(1−2α)) + ln(1/ε)/(1−2α)) O((ln(1/ε) + D t λ)/(1−2α) + (D t λ)²) SPECTRE converges slightly faster than KNIGHT when no attack is visible, the same expression minus KNIGHT's extra (D t λ)² term, but SPECTRE does not guarantee convergence once an attack is visible: it solves only "weak liveness," securing payments whose ordering among honest users is commutative, not the general consensus problem KNIGHT solves (§1, closing paragraph, citing [19]). Nakamoto Consensus's tolerable attacker share shrinks toward zero as D·λ grows: the table's own denominator, max{0, (1−α)/(1+D t λ) − α}, heads to zero as D t λ increases, which §3.1-3.2 calls "not scalable, since its security threshold deteriorates as the block creation rate λ grows." PHANTOM converges only in terms of D max , a worst-case latency chosen in advance, rather than the current D t that KNIGHT and SPECTRE track (§4: PHANTOM "converges in terms of D max = D only"). What this widget shows and does not show. The margin gauges (configured k, margin needed, in blocks) come straight from GHOSTDAG's own anticone-tolerance formula, verified exactly against rusty-kaspa's compiled table; k is a real protocol quantity, but this page does not simulate DAGKnight's actual k-cluster selection algorithm or vote count, a fair reading of the paper's qualitative Figure 4 (parameterized protocols hold a flat, hardcoded confirmation bound and can fail past it; parameterless ones track the current latency bound and stay safe, only slower), not a reproduction of it. The "confirmation bound" readouts, by contrast, are computed directly from the paper's own Table 1 and §1.5.2 optimistic (no-visible-attack) formula, the D max -versus-D t substitution described above; that formula has no unspecified constant, so those readouts are real numbers the paper commits to. The paper's separate, far rougher worst-case (visible-attack) bound, whose constant c the paper leaves unstated, sits one click down, labeled as a rough shape rather than a precise prediction, the same caveat the paper gives that bound past the point it calls "far from tight." The paper's own worked example (Figure 3, at λ = 3.75 bps, adversary share α = 0.2, confidence ε = 0.05) reports D = 2 s → k = 4, confirmation ≈ 12 s; D = 1 s → k = 1, confirmation ≈ 6 s; D = 0.1 s → k = 0, confirmation ≈ 1.2 s. Those three points use the paper's own tuned parameters, cited here for reference rather than wired into the sliders. Where the efficiency question is actually being worked: kaspanet's own branch, plus one contributor's personal fork and wiki. kaspanet/rusty-kaspa's own dagknight branch is active: latest commit "Merge branch 'dk-umc-proposed' into dagknight" , August 14, 2026, preceded by a run of [DK::UMC] and [DK::CZM] commits from August 12 to 14, 2026 (verified against the GitHub API commit log, checked 2026-08-22). Both coderofstuff (40 commits to the official repo) and freshair18 (9 commits) are credited contributors there, not outside parties. Separately, coderofstuff/rusty-kaspa is a personal fork carrying branches dagknight (last commit Jul 26, 2026), dkoder , dk-shortcut , dk-umc-proposed (last commit Aug 14, 2026, the same commit that merged into kaspanet's branch), and dk-with-tcp (last commit Aug 20, 2026). Its companion dk-wiki , unofficial and separate from kaspanet's own docs, states in 08-umc-voting.md (last edited Jul 24, 2026): "the paper's recursive algorithm as written still has worst-case O(n²) complexity, because in the worst case every block's vote must be computed and the recursion tree can be quadratic," and "If UMC voting is O(n²), the total rank search becomes O(n² × max_k), which is expensive." It proposes an incremental replacement it puts at "O(n × K) amortized." A related page, 06-rank.md (last edited Jul 31, 2026), describes a separate change that "reduces the number of k-colouring + UMC voting calls from O(max_k) to O(log(max_k))." A commit titled "[DK::bench] Add benchmarks for tie breaking" ( 73e3079 , May 28, 2026) adds a real criterion benchmark harness and fixture data testing tie-breaking at k = 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, and 53, but no measured output is committed anywhere: it is unrun benchmarking infrastructure, not a published number. The code itself has landed on kaspanet's own experimental branch; the analysis explaining why it matters has not. None of it is peer-reviewed, merged to master, or adopted as Kaspa's shipped algorithm. Sources: Sompolinsky, Bitcoin Takeover Podcast , S17 E36 (31:06), on the K-parameter/confirmation-time tradeoff going from 10 to 100 blocks/sec (citation supplied directly by this page's editor from the episode; the individual episode page was not independently located as of 2026-08-24, so the show's own listing is linked instead) · Sompolinsky & Sutton, "The DAG KNIGHT Protocol: A Parameterless Generalization of Nakamoto Consensus," IACR ePrint 2022/1494 (esp. §1.2, §1.3, §1.4, §1.5.2, Theorem 14, Figures 3 to 4), last revised Feb 24, 2023 ( version history ) · KIP-2 , Status: Proposed, no technical revision since Nov 30, 2022, only a metadata commit in Jul 2025 · rusty-kaspa bps.rs , params.rs , constants.rs (checked 2026-08-22) · kaspanet/rusty-kaspa dagknight branch commit log (checked 2026-08-22, via GitHub API) · unofficial: coderofstuff/rusty-kaspa and dk-wiki (checked 2026-08-22) · this site's What is Kaspa and Status . KIP 1–6, the foundational batch (2 of 6 active) KIP Title Layer Status 1 Rewriting the full node in Rust Consensus, Node Implemented 2 Upgrade consensus to follow DAGKNIGHT Consensus, API/RPC Proposed 3 Block sampling for efficient DAA with high BPS Consensus Rejected 4 Sparse difficulty windows Consensus Active 5 Message signing Applications Active 6 Proof of Chain Membership Consensus, Applications Draft KIP 9–15, consensus and script-engine expansion (5 of 5 active) KIP Title Layer Status 9 Extended mass formula for mitigating state bloat Consensus, Mempool, P2P Active 10 New transaction opcodes for enhanced script functionality Consensus, Script Engine Active 13 Transient storage handling Consensus Active 14 The Crescendo The May 2025 upgrade that sped Kaspa's mainnet from one block a second to ten. hardfork Consensus Active 15 Canonical transaction ordering and sequencing commitments Consensus Active KIP 16–21, the Toccata batch (4 of 4 active) KIP Title Layer Status 16 ZK precompile opcode Consensus, Script Engine Active 17 Covenants A rule attached to a coin that the network itself checks on every spend, not a server's promise. and improved scripting capabilities Consensus, Script Engine Active 20 Covenant IDs Consensus, Script Engine Active 21 Partitioned sequencing commitment with O(activity) proving Consensus, Chain-Block UTXO Validation Active Baseline read from the KIP repository on August 22, 2026. This table refreshes from the repository when the page loads. KIPs 16, 17, 20, and 21 went Active July 15, 2026, when Toccata reached mainnet, via the pull requests that first proposed each: KIP-16 , KIP-17 , KIP-20 , KIP-21 . KIP-2, the DAGKnight upgrade, has stayed Proposed for years: devnet only, no testnet, no date. Eleven more KIPs sit open as pull requests, among them 7, 8, 11, 12, 18, 19, and 22 through 25, why the tables skip 6 to 9 and 10 to 13. KIP-7 (finality rules) and KIP-8 (headers-proof replacement) are two of those open pull requests, not withdrawn or reserved. Read the repository for full text. Conventions Kaspa Calls for Conventions Builder agreements on encoding, not protocol changes: three merged since July 15, 2026, all still marked Status: Draft in the document itself, none cleared the README's own bar for acceptance, a Comments-URI discussion window and consensus among implementers. Merged, Status: Draft (3) Proposal Opened State KCC-0001 covenant definition, concepts, byte layout and ABI 2026-07-15 Merged, Status: Draft KCC-0002 authority schemes for program ABIs 2026-07-20 Merged, Status: Draft KCC-0020 fungible token covenant specification 2026-07-15 Merged, Status: Draft Open pull requests (2) Proposal Opened State KCC-0402 covenant payment channels 2026-07-19 Open pull request KCC-0021 covenant token metadata specification 2026-07-23 Open pull request Both authors claim adoption evidence the repository itself does not carry: KCC-0021's author says kascov and the wallet KaspaRocket already use its metadata convention, and KCC-0402's author says a reference implementation, k402, has payment-channel transactions live on mainnet. Neither claim is independently confirmed; treat both as the author's word until a merge or an outside source backs them. Closed, not merged (2) Proposal Opened State KCC-0008 through KCC-0024 multi-token, token, and commerce standards 2026-07-25 Closed, not merged (three attempts) KCC-0025 license agreement 2026-07-28 Closed, not merged Baseline read from the KCC repository on August 22, 2026. This table refreshes from the repository when the page loads; the live fetch below only lists currently open pull requests, so the three merged drafts and the closed proposals stay as this baseline describes them. KCC-0001 defines the byte layout for a covenant, a rule attached to a coin. The covenant breaker demo attacks a vault covenant with an early withdrawal, a skipped recovery key, and a forged lookalike, and shows the exact rule that stops each one. KCC-0020 is the most argued-over thread on the builder forum, and its shape has already leaked into working code: the Argent compiler ships a kcc20_asset.ag example defining a transferable asset covenant, normal before acceptance, not acceptance itself. A token issued against it today inherits three known defects: a permanent supply-split consequence its co-authors partly defend and partly call a wrong pattern still needing a spec fix, one production deployment that admits partial conformance, and a launchpad already on its fourth incompatible template. Try it: update one holder's tokens and watch a payment to the other get refused for good You and Sam hold the same token. Right now any coin of yours equals any coin of Sam's. Update just one of you, and that stops being true, for good. A made-up token, used as an example. The standard is real; this token is not. You ⇄ Sam 9 coins. One shared supply. Update Sam's coins Reset Either of you could pay the other any amount. A coin is a coin. A price, a balance, an exchange listing: anything that assumed one supply of this token now has to track two. What the spec's own authors said about this This demo is a simplified stand-in for KCC-0020, a draft Kaspa token rule that lets an issuer update the state of some holders and not others. Issue #14, opened by Knitser on kaspanet/kccs, August 21, 2026, reports that this same mechanism permanently splits a token's supply once triggered. Two KCC-0020 co-authors replied. This is not a universal bug: one pattern below is defended as intended, a different one is conceded as a wrong pattern the standard does not yet handle. Knitser said on August 23, 2026 that the co-authors' explanation clears up his original concern; a pull request tightening the spec's wording is open but not merged. “My view is that the combination of extended state, alongside token-specific entry points, allows for various use cases which are not only write-once, nor only for a singleton token. The standard transfer function, though, is meant to transfer fungible tokens, hence, it assumes that inputs and outputs state (excluding ownership and amount) must be identical (or else could not be treated as fungible)” Sivan Helfer (Manyfestation), KCC-0020 co-author · github.com/kaspanet/kccs/issues/14 “I can relate bcs example extensions that come to mind indeed illustrate this. for instance a frozen bool indicator which can be used by stable coin issuer for black listing, indeed renders the token as temporarily non fungible.” Michael Sutton, KCC-0020 co-author · github.com/kaspanet/kccs/issues/14 “I had one conceptual exception, but I think it means it's a wrong pattern. The example would be some contract using the ext state for storing receipt-like information… It mutates all the time but isn't part of the state that matters. I guess this pattern only makes sense if it was well defined as part of the std, and not as an opaque virtual state” Michael Sutton, KCC-0020 co-author · github.com/kaspanet/kccs/issues/14 “I agree that kind of pattern should either be defined in the standard or implemented in a non state storage (maybe the payload, as you once suggested).” Sivan Helfer (Manyfestation), KCC-0020 co-author · github.com/kaspanet/kccs/issues/14 KCC-0020 (Fungible Token Covenant Specification), authors Sivan Helfer, Michael Sutton, and Romain Billot, Status: Draft as of August 21, 2026. No spec change has merged as of this writing. Source: github.com/kaspanet/kccs/blob/main/kcc-0020.md . The supply-split consequence, defended in part, conceded in part Issue #14 , opened August 21, 2026 by Knitser and still open, shows that KCC-0020's transfer consolidation rule requires every input to carry the same extended-state commitment, but its state-update entrypoint can only be authorized by each cell's own holder, not the issuer, so there is no way to move every holder's cell to a new commitment at once. Update some cells and not others and the token's supply splits into groups that can never consolidate again, permanently. Co-authors Manyfestation and Michael Sutton defend one version of this as intended: Sutton's own stablecoin-blacklist example, where a frozen flag deliberately "renders the token as temporarily non fungible." But Sutton then flagged a second pattern, extended state used for ephemeral, receipt-like data that mutates without affecting fungibility, as "a wrong pattern," and both co-authors agreed it should either be defined in the standard or moved out of state entirely. A fourth commenter, ShawnPearce, added on August 23, 2026 that the standard's other candidate home for that data, the transaction payload, has its own catch: the v1 sighash commits the payload unconditionally, so it is signature-bound and transaction-scoped rather than per-cell, and under this spec's borrowed receive, a borrower who signs the transaction controls the payload the owner's cell gets recreated with. Knitser replied on August 23, 2026 that the co-authors' explanation "clears it up": an entrypoint that changes extended state makes a different type of token out of those specific cells rather than updating the original, so neither of his two originally proposed fixes was right. He then asked the spec text to say this more plainly in four places: the commitment wording, how balances display across commitment values, which entrypoints may change a commitment and under what authority, and how to handle receipt-like data. Manyfestation opened a pull request the same day, "Clarify KCC20 extended state fungibility semantics" ( #16 ), to cover it. The issue is still open and the pull request has not merged. The one production implementer's own conformance admission Issue #11 , opened July 26, 2026 by KaspaCom, is the only production implementer of a KCC token standard stating its own conformance level in writing: KaspaCom's deployed KCC20V2 "should be described as partially aligned, not fully conforming" with KCC-0001, 0002, 0020, and 0021. KaspaCom closed the issue itself on August 22, 2026, after the KCC-0021 author explained that its metadata layer is deliberately behavior-independent and does not require byte-for-byte KCC-0020 conformance to adopt. That answers KaspaCom's question; it does not withdraw the partial-conformance statement on the record above. Two more gaps: a forking launchpad template, and dead metadata links The standard's own template shape is already fragmenting on mainnet: one launchpad's 74 live tokens span four separate template generations, with no migration path between them, only opt-in burn and reissue, according to a kas-smiths.org post from 0xKnitser on August 15, 2026. Covenant tokens have no metadata standard on mainnet without KCC-0021, which stays an open, unmerged pull request, so name, ticker, and image all live off-chain today: the same 0xKnitser post cross-checked one live launchpad's logos and found 5 of 19 dead within days, 3 more serving HTML instead of an image. A second open gap in the same spec: borrowed receive Shawn described it on the kas-smiths.org forum, July 10, 2026: "borrowed receive lets anyone change your UTXO's outpoint, which griefs pre-signed, outpoint bound transactions." Borrowing a token into a UTXO before a pre-signed spend lands invalidates the transaction and forces a rebuild, with no signature-level fix. A month later Shawn explained why: "the v1 sighash folds the spent input's own outpoint into the signed message unconditionally," and AnyoneCanPay "only zeroes the other inputs' outpoints, never the signed input's own." Authorization has to move to something the covenant checks against its own state, not the transaction signature; nothing has merged. Read the KCC repository , or follow the discussion on kas-smiths.org . A status word here marks where something sits in this process, never that it works; for what is actually running, use the live status page . Keep reading Next pages Previous Kaspa mining Why Kaspa price and hash rate move on different clocks, and how to point your own ASIC at your own node.
