Status Kaspa current status What is live, targeted, roadmap, and research on Kaspa right now, checked against mainnet, releases, and KIPs.

pages.title: Kaspa Origin Story: Fair Launch, Failed Plans, and Crescendo | Kaspa Explained
pages.h1: Kaspa's fair launch was the path left after the other paths failed
pages.description: How Kaspa got here, from a research paper to a fair launch to a live smart contract layer.
pages.text: Origin story Kaspa's fair launch was the path left after the other paths failed Kaspa's launch structure was not chosen. It was what was left after research into faster proof-of-work ordering ran through DAGLabs and an April 2021 testnet, then through a hardware plan, a presale, and a DeFi pitch, each of which fell apart. Every earlier structure would have made Kaspa answer to something outside the protocol. Fair launch took the premine, the pre-sale, and the insider table off the starting line before mainnet existed, and it proved nothing about later adoption, price, or whether the tech would work. See it Kaspa's zero, plotted against three other launches Try it: plot Kaspa's zero-premine supply against three other launches Every chain set a rule for who'd hold the first coins, at block zero. Drag the year marker to see who held what. What matters is how long the grip lasts. Founders, company, or foundation share Kaspa Ethereum Cardano XRP Ethereum and Cardano funded a foundation; XRP had no public sale at all. Kaspa: 0%. No founder, company, or foundation has ever held a share. DAGLabs, the founders' own company, mined an estimated 2.5–3% of supply after launch, the same way anyone with hardware could. Solid: documented history. Dashed, past the marker: modeled projection. Year since genesis 0 Fade speed (modeled, not measured) i More about fade speed Models how fast a founder's or company's share shrinks toward today's figure, mostly through selling and spending. 1.0× anchors that to each chain's current estimate. Kaspa has no such share to fade. 1.0× Reset Tracks founders, company, and foundation shares only. DAGLabs' own early mining is a separate question, covered below. Chain Founders/company held Public / open Status at this year What a premine Coins created and held before launch, before anyone else could mine or buy them. buys, and what Kaspa's launch looked like See the number above. What's not settled is how DAGLabs' own early mining split between Polychain and the team; full sourcing below. Full launch history, assumptions, and sources Runs entirely in your browser. Research first The problem came before the coin Bitcoin at high block rates has one weak point: two honest miners can solve a block seconds apart, and the single-chain rule throws one of those blocks' work away. Kaspa's research line starts from that exact waste. A blockDAG keeps both blocks visible instead of dropping one, then uses a rule like GHOSTDAG to order that graph into one shared history. The papers behind it DBLP lists Yonatan Sompolinsky and Aviv Zohar's 2018 paper, PHANTOM: A Scalable BlockDAG Protocol , as an IACR ePrint paper, sitting on the same blockDAG research line as SPECTRE before it. A July 2017 Epicenter episode with Zohar and Sompolinsky describes SPECTRE as dropping the blockchain data structure so blocks can be made all the time and merged after. No one races for one slot. DAGLabs and testnet DAGLabs came first, then the fair launch DAGLabs was co-founded by Yonatan Sompolinsky and Guy Corem. It paid for and ran part of the pre-mainnet path: a Golang build of Phantom/GHOSTDAG, then an April 2021 public testnet. There was no token premine, but there was a VC-funded backstory that shaped the hardware, mining, and fair-launch debate before mainnet existed. Founding date dispute, testnet bundle, and the code's real origin Public sources disagree on when DAGLabs was founded. An April 26, 2021 Investing.com launch article says 2017, with $8 million raised from Polychain and Accomplice. The HackerNoon interview intro says Sompolinsky founded DAGLabs in 2018. Guy Corem's April 13, 2021 testnet note calls Kaspa a Golang build of Phantom/GHOSTDAG and a broader form of Nakamoto Consensus. The testnet bundle: full node, web wallet, faucet, Katnip block explorer, graph inspector, Kashboard, framed as testnet first, mainnet later, no pre-mining or founder allocations planned. Yonatan's Hashdag Kaspa co-founder Yonatan Sompolinsky's research writing site, where he lays out design ideas ahead of protocol work. archive describes the original Kaspad codebase as built from the Bitcoin client btcd , written in Golang. That holds up; the unsourced "Bitcoin Core 0.19" claim floating around does not. Could-have-been paths Failed plans are part of the story An ASIC Application-specific integrated circuit: a chip built to do one job, in Kaspa's case running kHeavyHash, fast. It cannot be reprogrammed for anything else the way a general-purpose CPU or GPU can. -and-presale plan, a DeFi-sequencing pitch, and a flawed gamenet all came before the fair launch, and none of them worked out. What each failed path actually was ASIC and presale path Hashdag's 2020 archive said Kaspa would have no premine or founder rewards, then called DAGLabs a for-profit miner with a pre-launch ASIC-tuning path and a DeFi-contract auction for rights to future Kaspa coins. Yonatan later said that path never happened: the optical ASIC chips it leaned on weren't ready. DeFi sequencing path The April 2021 launch article framed Kaspa as faster ordering rails for DeFi apps on Ethereum. The Uphold interview recap agrees: Kaspa's focus is sequencing, where transaction order and MEV move real money. Neither is a claim Kaspa ever shipped as an Ethereum L2. Gamenet path Yonatan later called the gamenet attempt flawed: closer to a testnet with rewards bolted on than a real mainnet. Fair-launch path In the HackerNoon interview, Yonatan called DAGLabs a failed attempt to square venture-backed and fair-launch models; investors pushed for launch with no business model or ROI plan. Asked if Polychain pushed him to launch, he agreed, and added that Gadi pushed too, because he saw the promise. "Solana-like" developer experience The comparison comes from Yonatan's own interviews, and it points at developer and user experience: one cohesive, Rust-friendly toolchain that feels fast to work in. It is not a claim about copying Solana's execution model, which Kaspa L1 does not share. Launch Mainnet launched without a premine Mainnet followed the April 2021 testnet within the year: a fair-launched Proof-of-Work network with no premine, insider allocation, or pre-sales. The node's own genesis record is the proof, not marketing copy: rusty-kaspa's genesis.rs ships a checkpoint DAA score and a UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. commitment that trace back to an empty genesis. Mining made the whole supply, but a fair launch didn't guarantee equal access to early mining. Yonatan's own archive is blunter than the lore: the launch was messy, he baked several bad ideas into the first gamenet rules, and a few thousand CPUs found the project within days, pushing hashrate up no matter what the plan wanted. The Black Tuesday post puts it in one clause: the gamenet idea never caught air, so he swapped the random block reward for a flat one. Early-miner share estimate Yonatan later estimated Kaspa's core developers mined about 2.5% of total supply after launch; the Kaspa Wiki prehistory page puts the related DAGLabs/Polychain estimate below 3%, roughly 840 million KAS, tightening to closer to 2.5% and under 850 million KAS. That's early-miner context, a separate question from whether there was a premine. Early stress Kaspa had to survive real failure On November 23, 2021, Yonatan published "Kaspa (Black Tuesday)" after a network crash in the 48 hours before. His account: the developers were rebuilding against a known-valid UTXO commitment after a memory problem, not rolling back to a state they liked better. That is the sourced version of the "two-week bug" story. The genesis rusty-kaspa still ships is dated November 22, 2021, the day before the post, putting the real outage at days, not the two weeks the story usually claims. The repair in the code, and the September 2023 dust attack The repair is in the code. Kaspad's November 2021 hard-fork commit is titled "new genesis with the utxo set of the last block." The mainnet genesis block carries a DAA score of 1,312,860 marked as a checkpoint, plus the same UTXO commitment hash the post published. A separate dust attack on Yom Kippur, September 2023, is a different event. Kaspa researcher Shai Wyborski's post-mortem gives the method: each attack transaction spent one UTXO and created 238, adding about 1,185 entries per block at roughly 85 bytes each, near 100 KB of lasting state per block, about 5 GB a day. He counted 57 million attacker UTXOs created before September 28: "5GB of junk UTXO data we will have to carry permanently." The fix was KIP Kaspa Improvement Proposal: the process that specifies, reviews, and merges a protocol change. Nothing on this site counts as shipped without a merged KIP and a release tag. -9's extended mass formula, which prices state growth into transaction mass. The attacker now pays for the state they create. Rust, Crescendo, Toccata Golang was not the final version Hashdag's 2022 "Kaspa where to" archive says Michael Sutton pushed for a big refactor and Rust rewrite, because the Golang code carried old debt that made it hard for new coders to work in; how the rewrite was funded is not known here. The rusty-kaspa repo describes the Rust build as a drop-in replacement for the older Golang node. Its README puts the Crescendo hard fork on May 5, 2025, moving the network from 1 BPS to 10 BPS; the v1.0.0 release notes name the exact trigger, mainnet DAA score 110,165,000. "Toccata" gets pinned on 10 BPS often enough to be worth fixing. Crescendo is the fork that made 10 BPS live on mainnet. Toccata is separate and later: base-layer code support with covenants, Silverscript, ZK Zero-knowledge: a proof that a statement is true without revealing the data behind it, so a script can accept a claim about work done elsewhere without seeing that work. -facing proof checks, sequencing commitments, and native-asset groundwork, turned on at DAA score 474,165,565. Rusty Kaspa v2.0.0 shipped that switch, v2.0.1 followed as the Toccata release; wallet, indexer, and app use are still building, so check the status page for where each stands. Try it: convert a DAA score to a date, and catch a lying timestamp Kaspa's clock counts blocks, not seconds, at two different speeds since Crescendo. Drag the slider and read a block's real date. 1. Read a DAA score A DAA score rises by about one per accepted block, not once a second: 1 block a second before Crescendo (5 May 2025), 10 after. This converter switches rate exactly at that boundary, marked below. Crescendo genesis today and beyond DAA score Two exact points anchor this: genesis and Toccata's activation. Rates between them come from real elapsed time, not the bare protocol target. Dates after Toccata are an estimate assuming today's rate holds. Jump to genesis Jump to Crescendo Jump to Toccata Jump to today A separate demo: catch a miner lying about a block's time Catch a lying timestamp A miner who backdates a block can make it look like blocks are arriving slower than they are, and cheapen mining by lowering the difficulty. So every timestamp is checked: it must land after the middle time of the block's last 11 ancestors , and can't sit more than 132 seconds ahead of the checking node's clock. refused: too old accepted refused: too far ahead Bitcoin checks time almost the same way Bitcoin uses the same 11-block median floor, but allows a timestamp up to 2 hours ahead of now. Kaspa allows only 132 seconds: it expects a new block every tenth of a second, not every 10 minutes. Bitcoin, how far ahead a timestamp can be 2 hours (7,200s) Kaspa, how far ahead a timestamp can be 132 seconds How this is worked out, and where the numbers come from DAA score is a block count, not a timer Each block inherits its selected parent's DAA score and adds the number of new blocks in its own merge set that qualify for the difficulty window: daa_score = parent_daa_score + (mergeset_size - mergeset_non_daa_count) . Source: consensus/src/processes/difficulty.rs , function internal_calc_daa_score , in kaspanet/rusty-kaspa . Why the old converter was wrong, and what changed A single flat rate, 10 DAA units per second, does not hold all the way back through history, even anchored on Toccata's activation. Kaspa's own consensus config shows that rate only held after Crescendo: consensus/core/src/config/params.rs sets mainnet's pre_crescendo_target_time_per_block to 1000 milliseconds (1 block per second) and its post-Crescendo target_time_per_block to 100 milliseconds (10 blocks per second), with crescendo_activation at DAA score 110,165,000. A flat 10-per-second rate applied to a pre-Crescendo score overstates elapsed time by roughly 10x for every day, which is many months of error for anything mined before 5 May 2025. The converter now switches rates at that boundary and interpolates between three real anchors: Kaspa's mainnet genesis (DAA 0, an exact protocol constant), Crescendo's activation (DAA 110,165,000, near 5 May 2025, 15:00 UTC per Kaspa's own activation announcement), and Toccata's mainnet activation (DAA 474,165,565, an exact date from the release notes). The date conversion used above Genesis anchors the pre-Crescendo segment; Toccata anchors the post-Crescendo segment; both are exact. The rate within each segment is the real elapsed time between its two anchors divided by the DAA units between them, not the bare protocol target, so the two segments meet with no jump at the Crescendo boundary. That interpolation puts the actual average between Crescendo and Toccata at about 0.06% off the 10-per-second target across 421 days, which is the basis for calling the post-Crescendo approximation good, not exact. Dates after Toccata extrapolate forward at the 10-per-second target rate, since there's no later anchor yet. Timestamp rules used above Past median time: a block's timestamp must be strictly greater than the median of the 11 values closest to the center of a sampled window of its ancestors' timestamps. Source: consensus/src/processes/past_median_time.rs , constant AVERAGE_FRAME_SIZE = 11 , implementing KIP-0004, Sparse Difficulty Windows . A timestamp at or before that median fails with RuleError::TimeTooOld , checked in consensus/src/pipeline/header_processor/post_pow_validation.rs . Future bound: a header is rejected if its timestamp is more than 132 seconds ahead of the validating node's own clock, failing with RuleError::TimeTooFarIntoTheFuture . Source: consensus/src/pipeline/header_processor/pre_ghostdag_validation.rs ( max_block_time = unix_now() + timestamp_deviation_tolerance * 1000 ), constant defined as TIMESTAMP_DEVIATION_TOLERANCE = 132 in consensus/core/src/config/constants.rs . Why the median is sampled, not walked Bitcoin's 11 ancestors form a straight line: block 100 always follows block 99. Kaspa's DAG lets many blocks get mined in parallel and then merge together, so there's no single line of 11 to walk. Instead the median comes from a sampled window across the blocks the network has already folded in, defined by KIP-0004 above. Blocks that arrive at nearly the same moment from different miners can all raise the DAA score together and all count toward that window; none of them is "block 100" on its own. Bitcoin's rule, checked against its own source Bitcoin Core rejects a block whose time is at or before GetMedianTimePast() , the median of the 11 preceding blocks ( nMedianTimeSpan = 11 ), with the reject reason time-too-old . It also rejects a block timestamped more than MAX_FUTURE_BLOCK_TIME (2 hours, 7,200 seconds) ahead of the node's own clock, with reject reason time-too-new . Source: bitcoin/bitcoin , src/chain.h ( nMedianTimeSpan , MAX_FUTURE_BLOCK_TIME ) and src/validation.cpp (the two checks, near CheckBlockHeader / ContextualCheckBlockHeader ). pages.title: Kaspa Design Case | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: What Kaspa is trying to be: money nobody can quietly change the rules on, that still settles fast.
pages.text: Kaspa's design case Answer Crypto earns its keep when people need one shared record and no single operator running it. Kaspa's bet is that Bitcoin-style Proof-of-Work Miners spend real computation to propose blocks. security and censorship resistance can run closer to real time without giving up either one. Start with the job Five jobs, Kaspa at a different stage on each. The five-job table Crypto job Kaspa angle Status Self-custodied money Fair-launched Proof-of-Work UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. asset with direct wallet control. Live Fast payment feel 10 BPS blockDAG A graph where multiple honest blocks exist in parallel instead of a single forced line. gets a payment into a block faster than slow PoW chains. Live, with confirmation tradeoffs One shared record GHOSTDAG orders parallel honest blocks in a DAG. Live Assets with rules Toccata put spend rules, ZK hooks, sequencing commitments, and vProgs groundwork into L1. Covenant rules live on L1; wallet and app evidence next. See Programmability, below , for what builders get today. Group commitments Base Real-Time Decentralization (RTD) today. RTD-derived attestations, oracles, and TangVM A proposed add-on, not yet built, that would let a smart contract watch outside data and trigger itself instead of waiting for someone to trigger it by hand. come later. Base idea live; app systems still future work Rare combination What the other networks are already good at Bitcoin has the longest track record as a store of value. Ethereum has the deepest pool of smart contracts. Solana has the most polished fast-app feel. Kaspa leads on none of the three today; its claim is a combination none of them make: mined issuance, fixed supply, blocks that arrive in parallel, and app rules on that same base layer. A paragraph can't rank them honestly; the chain comparer does, scoring twenty layer ones, family by family, on fields measured the same day. Pick your constraint Every design pays for its wins somewhere No crypto design gets speed, security, privacy, and a network nobody controls. Push on one and the cost lands somewhere else. Map Table Speed feedback Security cost Many verifiers friction Privacy hidden data Usability recovery Improve one corner and another gives. Goal Why people want it What it costs Decentralization No easy single control point. Harder upgrades, worse UX, slower agreement, more on you. Security Hard-to-fake history and valid supply. Fees, power bills, staked capital, and a security budget that holds up. Speed Fast inclusion and better user feedback. Blocks clash more, nodes get heavier, checks thin out, control narrows. Privacy Less watching. Every coin spends the same. Heavier math, bigger data, harder to audit, fewer exchanges. Self-custody You hold the keys. No company account. No password reset, no chargeback, no support line. Why a public chain can't just be Visa-fast Visa settles fast because nobody outside Visa has to check its work: banks, contracts, one company's servers, and a fraud team handle that internally, and Visa can undo errors, block users, and change the rules at will. A public chain asks thousands of strangers to check the same rules, with no one in charge, so independent nodes can throw out bad history without asking anyone. That is the slow part. The app layer can be Visa-fast; a base layer anyone can check cannot. Concentration arrives by a different door in each model. ASIC cost gathers around whoever has the capital, the cheap power, and the chips. Proof of stake skips the hardware, so holding the token buys the say instead. Every one of those costs still lands on Kaspa. The bet it makes against them is narrow, and it starts with keeping the blocks that lose the race. Latency, inclusion, and confirmation Bitcoin proved strangers can agree on scarce digital money with nobody in charge. It pays for that with a slow block interval, picked partly because network lag has to stay small next to block production. Kaspa comes out of the research line asking whether mining work that a single chain throws away as a collision can count toward consensus instead. Any fast block-producing system can get a transaction into a block quickly. That's inclusion. It says nothing about confirmation: how fast the network gives strong confidence the transaction won't reverse. Mixing the two up is the most common way "fast blockchain" claims mislead. How GHOSTDAG and real-time decentralization work Every Nakamoto-style system carries Bitcoin's latency tradeoff by design. RTD Hashdag's framing: Bitcoin-style PoW security operating in real time. , Real-Time Decentralization, is Hashdag Kaspa co-founder Yonatan Sompolinsky's research writing site, where he lays out design ideas ahead of protocol work. 's term for a partially synchronous system that moves as fast as the network really allows: fast when conditions are clean, slower but still safe when the network is struggling or under attack. Blue work is what makes it measurable, letting nodes compare total work across a graph instead of a single chain. See how GHOSTDAG colors and orders that graph and try the live version there. Storage-mass pricing charges a transaction for the UTXO footprint it leaves behind for good, on top of its raw size. Pruning and bounded anticones cap what a node has to hold and how far the parallel edges can spread, which is what lets an ordinary machine keep up with a fast proof-of-work DAG. Hashdag points that speed at shared commitments instead of price charts. The simplest version is Kickstarter-like funding, where money moves only if enough people commit and a public rule holds the threshold instead of a company that can wave it away. How Bitcoin, Kaspa, Ethereum, and Solana split on this Proof of Stake usually gets fast finality by quickly counting votes from staked validators, which ties confirmation speed to how well those validators coordinate and how the stake is spread. On Solana a stake-weighted schedule picks which validator leads each slot and puts the transactions in order. Push decentralization further and that job gets harder, which often drives the system toward committees or other sampling shortcuts. Proof of Work samples security a different way. A block is proof the finder beat the rest of the network's hash power for that round, so the protocol never has to poll most of the miners before it confirms anything. Block speed and miner headcount come apart. The two models also split on cost. Proof of Work brings outside cost into consensus, in power bills and hardware. Proof of Stake backs the ledger with token ownership inside the system instead. That gap changes who can censor, how new coins are issued, and what an attack costs. "10 BPS" by itself is not the claim. K, finality depth, and merge depth all scale with the block rate, and they are what keep high block production from turning into runaway parallelism. less stake-vote coordination Bitcoin slow inclusion, PoW confirmations Kaspa fast inclusion, PoW confirmations Ethereum PoS finality, committee sampling Solana fast UX, stake-vote finality faster inclusion Reversal odds fall as blue work stacks up. Drive the wait time below and watch Kaspa's confirmation curve move against Bitcoin's. Waiting is what makes a payment safe, not the block count. Drag to change how strong the attacker is, and watch how long each chain needs. How much mining power the attacker controls: weak, 1% past the 50% line, 60% how careful you want to be relaxed normal strict A reorg is not paperwork. If the block carrying your payment gets replaced, the attacker can spend the same coins again elsewhere. That double-spend is what this wait protects against. Safe means the attacker has lost the race to out-mine your payment, a chance that falls the longer you wait. Kaspa's separate finality rule blocks any reorg past 432,000 blocks (12 hours), no matter the attacker's share; how the two differ is below. Three chains, same three this site compares everywhere: Bitcoin and Litecoin as classic single-chain proof of work at different speeds, Kaspa as the fast blockDAG this site explains. The model, and where the Kaspa line is an approximation Model. This is the "double-spend race" from Satoshi Nakamoto's Bitcoin whitepaper, section 11 (2008). An attacker holding a share of the network's mining power races to out-produce the blocks already confirming a payment. The whitepaper models that race as a Poisson process and asks: what is the chance the attacker still catches up after z blocks. P(z) = 1 − ∑ k=0 z Poisson(k; λ)·(1 − (q/p) z−k ), λ=z·q/p, q

pages.title: Why Parallel Spends Don't Collide | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Two demos: spend a UTXO wallet, then compose two apps together. Why a coin never has to queue behind another spender the way an account balance does.
pages.text: Two models, side by side Why parallel spends don't collide An account balance is one slot two spenders can fight over. A UTXO Unspent transaction output. Value sits in separate coins, spent whole and replaced by new ones, instead of living in one account balance that gets edited. coin isn't. Two demos below show why. Try it: the collision Who wins the same slot Send two spenders after the same balance, two coins, or one coin twice. Account model 1,240 KAS UTXO model (Kaspa) 4 coins, 1,240 KAS total Pay a little Pay a lot Combine coins Split in two Reset One balance, four coins. Pick a move. Two spenders, one moment Same account balance Two different coins The same coin twice Pick one A Spender A B Spender B Pick one. Why UTXO parallelizes, and the honest tradeoff Shared, mutable state is what the account model is built to handle: two calls into one balance just need to line up in order, which is why broad contracts landed there first. A coin carries no shared slot to line up, which is why UTXO checks can run at once and a block rate like Kaspa's is possible without having to invent account locks. Why UTXO parallelizes and an account model doesn't A payment from an account has to read the current balance, subtract, and write the new balance back, in that order, for that one account. A second payment from the same account has to wait for the first to finish, or the two writes race and the balance goes wrong. That order is a property of the model, not a performance bug: any two spends on the same shared number must be ordered somehow. A UTXO carries no such shared number. Two coins that belong to two people are two pieces of state. Spending one has nothing to say about spending the other, so a network checking many blocks in parallel can accept both without syncing with each other. That is why a ledger built on coins scales better with block rate: the thing that would need locking in an account model, one shared balance, doesn't exist. Kaspa's blockDAG accepts many blocks in parallel and orders them with GHOSTDAG; a payment system built on separate coins is the shape that fits a high block rate without inventing a way to lock each account. The one case where UTXO can't parallelize is the same coin spent twice. That's a real conflict, not a queue: just one of the two spends is kept, and the other loses outright. Kaspa settles this with a fixed rule: the first spend of a coin to appear in the ordered record wins, and any later clashing spend loses. Every node runs the same rule over the same DAG and lands on the same answer with no voting round. The honest cost: broad contracts The account model's shared, mutable, openly readable balance is really the easier shape for any contract. One contract can hold state, and any other contract can call into it, read that state, and change it, all in the same transaction, because there is one address with one storage slot others can point at. That's what makes something like Ethereum's account based virtual machine a good home for composable, broad logic. UTXO has no matching shared slot. State lives split up across many coins, and a script can inspect only the spend touching it. It cannot call another coin the way one contract calls another. Writing a broad, composable smart contract platform directly on top of that is really harder. That's the reason Kaspa's own contract story runs through covenants , not a broad account based virtual machine. A covenant is a rule attached to a coin about how it, and what it makes, are allowed to be spent, checked by script level checks on the spend itself. Post-Toccata mainnet Kaspa has covenants, covenant IDs, and ZK Zero-knowledge: a proof that a statement is true without revealing the data behind it, so a script can accept a claim about work done elsewhere without seeing that work. proof checks enforced at the script level. There is no account based VM underneath any of it. Kaspa's push past that stays inside the one spend being checked, not a shared slot other spends can reach into whenever they like. KIP-16 added an opcode that checks a ZK proof inside a spend, so a script can accept a claim about work done elsewhere without replaying it. Argent's Inter-Covenant Communication uses covenant IDs and checks to let one app's actor allow or watch another's, but only inside a single atomic spend both apps get spent and remade in, and it has shipped so far only in unaudited offline demos. vProgs, aimed at the harder case of many users sharing one app's state across many spends, is a plan with zero releases as of this writing. None of it is an account VM. How far that combining reaches today is its own demo, below. Source rusty-kaspa, consensus/core/src/tx.rs Establishes A transaction input names a previous output's outpoint (a whole prior output, fully used); a transaction output carries a value and an optional covenant binding. That's the basic reason for "whole coin in, change coin out." Does not establish Wallet UX, fee mechanics, or how any specific wallet chooses which coins to spend. Source KIP-17, Covenants and Improved Scripting Capabilities and KIP-20, Covenant IDs , both listed Active on this site's KIP tracker Establishes Covenants work by script level check opcodes that read fields of the spending transaction (amounts, script public keys, input/output counts) and constrain how a coin can be spent. This is the mechanism, not a broad callable virtual machine. Does not establish Broad wallet support for building covenant transactions, or that native DeFi or vProgs app throughput are live today; this site's claim fact-check keeps those labeled apart. UTXO vs. account model status: kaspanet/rusty-kaspa (see this site's claim fact-check , entry utxo ). First spend wins conflict rule: this site's what-is-kaspa page, sourced to Kaspa Research (GHOSTDAG ordering). Toccata went live with covenants, covenant IDs, and ZK proof checks at DAA score 474,165,565, per the rusty-kaspa v2.0.0 release . The ZK verifier opcode is KIP-16, OpZkPrecompile , and its status is Active. So far, Inter-Covenant Communication has shipped only in unaudited, offline demos, per argent-lang/argent . vProgs, plan stage, zero releases: kaspanet/vprogs . Try it: race for one slot Race for the exact same data One value, two writers, right now: on UTXO, then on an account model. Kaspa: UTXO Account model Only one writer can land here. – You Rival you rival Grab it One shared slot. Both want it now. A separate, harder question: can two apps compose? Can two apps compose across spends? Same transaction Many users vProgs Possible today, in one spend only. App A App B App C One app can act on another's, inside a single spend. Shipped only in unaudited demos. Why this happens, and what Toccata actually shipped Kaspa: UTXO. A payment, a token balance, or an app's data on Kaspa lives in one owned, one time spendable cell (a UTXO). Two spends can both target that same cell at once, the way you and the rival just did. Only one confirms. The network does not compare which one paid more or arrived "more validly"; it resolves by which one lands first. The other is rejected outright and has to rebuild against what is left, not merge with the winner and not wait in line behind it. Account model. Ethereum and similar chains track a running balance or contract state instead of coins spent just once. Two writers to the very same account do not need to reject one another the same way: both actions can apply, one after the other, in whatever order the network settles on. Nobody's write is thrown out just for arriving second; it just lands after the first one instead of in place of it. That behavior, order rather than rejection, is the account side half of the same question this page asks. This is a simple model of outpoint contention and of account style sequencing, not real network timing (mempool spread, block ordering, gas and fee markets). What blocks the double spend. Nothing stops two clashing spends from being broadcast in the first place: a wallet can sign and send two spends against the same coin, and the network does not check for that at broadcast time. What cannot happen is both landing in the kept state. It is not a single block rule: a block cannot hold two of its own spends of the same coin, rusty-kaspa's consensus turns that block down outright. But Kaspa is a DAG, so the real race is usually between two blocks landing at the same time, not two spends in one block. GHOSTDAG orders every block into one sequence first, then each block's spends are replayed in that order against a running UTXO diff; whichever spend lands earlier in that order wins, the other block stays valid and stays in the DAG, but its clashing spend fails validation against the state it is checked against and never joins the kept set. That after-the-fact order is also why two actions on separate coins cannot be made to depend on each other the way two calls into one shared account can: each spend is checked against a snapshot GHOSTDAG fixes later, not against a promise that the other side will also succeed. Sources: rusty-kaspa's block body double spend check and the mergeset acceptance loop that orders and replays spends by GHOSTDAG before applying them to the UTXO diff. What Toccata put on mainnet for this. Three of the KIPs Toccata turned on are the live primitives the panel above runs on. KIP-17 gives a script's check opcodes over the spend touching it: it can read that spend's own inputs, outputs, and payload, not some other spend's. KIP-20 adds covenant IDs, a lineage tag tracked by consensus an output can only carry by continuing a covenant or genesis-initializing a fresh one, so one covenant's record can't be forged. KIP-16 adds an opcode that checks a ZK proof inside a spend, useful for taking a claim about work done without replaying it. None of the three lets a script reach out and read a different covenant's live state the way a function call reads another contract's storage on an account chain; that reading stays scoped to the one spend now being checked. What composition permits, and why the block doesn't matter. Two apps built apart can compose today, but only inside a single spend that remakes both of them at once. Argent's Inter-Covenant Communication works this way: one app's actor allows or watches another's, and it works because both apps' state sits in the readable inputs and outputs of that one spend. It has shipped so far only in unaudited offline demos, per Argent's README; anyone who says an Argent app is running on Kaspa mainnet today is saying something that has not happened. The line that matters is the spend, not the block: sharing a block with other spends does not link them, the same way two spends in different blocks are no less composed than two in the same block would be. KIP-21's partitioned sequencing lanes (Status: Active) scale how much of that throughput a block can carry; they do not change what a single spend can bind together. Sources: argent-lang/argent , KIP-17 , KIP-20 , KIP-16 , KIP-21 . vProgs, and its status. The gap those two don't close: many users writing to one shared app's state at once (an exchange pool, say), where combining apps on L1 today tends toward an exit style, settling when someone leaves rather than the moment they act. vProgs is a roadmap plan aimed at that gap, not a shipped feature: its own repo README opens with "This repository is in early development / prototype phase. APIs and architecture may change significantly," and as of this writing it carries zero releases and zero tags. Its own architect, Kaspa core developer Michael Sutton, frames the design tradeoff as a choice between "losing synchronous composability or losing sovereignty," and describes one target as "standalone, non-composable sovereign vprogs" settling back to L1 through their own way out, which is the tradeoff the panel shows. Sources: kaspanet/vprogs , Michael Sutton's based-apps design notes . Bitcoin-style PoW security and censorship resistance, with confirmations that feel seconds-scale on a normal network. hashd.ag/raw Toccata Live Hard fork for L1 spend rules, asset rules, Silverscript A higher-level language that compiles down to Kaspa script, so a covenant can be written as readable rules instead of hand-assembled opcodes. , ZK proof checks, and sequencing commitments. Activation record v2.0.0 published June 5, 2026 as the Mainnet Toccata Release, setting activation at DAA 474,165,565. v2.0.1 followed June 15, 2026 as the maintenance release, adding standalone based-zk apps and vProgs groundwork. v2.0.1 release ; v2.0.0 activation release ; Toccata guide ; tn10-toc3 release ; Kaspa KIPs vProgs Roadmap Apps that prove richer logic while sharing Kaspa ordering. L1 never becomes one global VM that runs everything. vProgs repo ; programmability docs Native DeFi Roadmap A design target that follows Toccata-era L1 foundations. A live Kaspa-native app layer needs shipped apps and real usage. Design case DAGKnight Research A parameterless consensus direction, meaning it adapts instead of being tuned by hand. It does not run mainnet today; GHOSTDAG does. KIP-2 , still Status: Proposed; hashd.ag 100 BPS / netsplit-resilient Describes a payment that would keep confirming correctly even if part of the network loses contact with the rest, a break called a netsplit. payments Research A proposed 2027 hard fork target: 10-millisecond blocks, 100 BPS, netsplit-resilient local payments. No spec, code, or release yet. Where this claim comes from Kaspa.org puts 10-millisecond blocks, 100 BPS, and netsplit-resilient local payments in a proposed 2027 hard fork. That page is the only place the claim appears, and this site does not treat it as a reliable source. No spec, code, release, or activation evidence exists anywhere else. No anchor source. The only place this appears is a kaspa.org roadmap page, which this site does not accept as a source. RTD-derived oracle / TangVM A proposed add-on, not yet built, that would let a smart contract watch outside data and trigger itself instead of waiting for someone to trigger it by hand. flows Research Apps can build oracle, TangVM, attestation, and coordination-market systems on top of Kaspa. The protocol ships none of them as products. hashd.ag/raw Is that Kaspa claim true? 16 claims, grouped by category, checked against the source behind each one on August 22, 2026 Last checked: August 22, 2026 against release tags, raw KIP and KCC files, project READMEs, and mainnet readings. Recheck at emission checkpoints, after new primary sources, or when wallet/app/tooling support changes. Core protocol Claim Status Why Kaspa is proof-of-work Live Why Kaspa is mined, proof-of-work, full stop. Source: rusty-kaspa . Kaspa is a blockDAG using GHOSTDAG Live Why GHOSTDAG orders parallel blocks into one history instead of discarding the losers. Source: GHOSTDAG page . Kaspa is 10 BPS Live Why 10 blocks per second, the Crescendo-era rate. Source: releases . Kaspa already runs at 100 BPS Research Why not 10 BPS is live. 100 BPS is an unconfirmed roadmap proposal with no release, KIP, or code behind it. The 100 BPS, sub-40ms-block proposal exists only in kaspa.org's roadmap prose, which this site does not treat as a citable source after it was caught describing Toccata as pre-mainnet eight weeks after mainnet activation. Source: unverified, flagged. Kaspa payments become irreversible immediately Wrong Why Inclusion is fast; confirmation confidence rises probabilistically over time. Source: finality page . Toccata and smart contracts Claim Status Why Toccata has activated on mainnet Live protocol Why Live, activated at DAA 474,165,565; v2.0.1 followed as the release. App, wallet, explorer, SDK, and user adoption are separate, still-open checks. Source: status table above . TN10 Testnet-10, one of Kaspa's test networks, where upgrades get tried out before they reach the live mainnet. Toccata test means mainnet activation Testnet only Why not No. tn10-toc2, tn10-toc3, and the Testnet-10 DAA evidence are testnet-only; v2.0.0 set the mainnet activation score. Source: v2.0.0 activation release . TN12 Testnet-12, a separate Kaspa test network used the same way as TN10: trying out changes before mainnet. proves mainnet covenants Testnet only What actually proves it Covenants are live on mainnet, but TN12 is not why. That claim rests on the v2.0.0 activation score; TN12 is testnet prototyping evidence. Kaspa has mature native smart contracts Not yet What's still ahead Toccata shipped the covenant and proof-check layer only. Mature native DeFi and full app infrastructure are still ahead, through later vProgs work. Tokenomics and standards Claim Status Why July 2026 is a sudden emission cliff Misleading Why Emission steps down by a fixed factor every 2,629,800 seconds. DAA score triggers the step. The calendar does not: 24.49971474 KAS/sec from 478,611,000, then 23.12465141 from 504,909,000, which the network passed around August 5 and where it still sits as of August 22, then 21.82676446 from 531,207,000, roughly early September. Source: tokenomics . KCC-0020 A Kaspa Call for Conventions: a proposal for how different Kaspa wallets and apps can agree on a shared format, like a token standard. It does not change Kaspa's consensus rules; a KIP does that. is a ratified fungible-token standard Not yet The defect and the one production implementer KCC-0001, KCC-0002, and KCC-0020 merged into the kccs repo, but each still reads Status: Draft in its own body. KCC-0020 also carries a permanent-supply-split consequence (issue #14): its transfer-consolidation rule and its extended-state update entrypoint contradict each other, so a token using the extended-state path can permanently split its own supply. Co-authors defend one pattern behind this as intended, a frozen or blacklist flag, but conceded a second pattern, ephemeral state that mutates without affecting fungibility, is a wrong one needing a spec fix. The reporter's concern stands unwithdrawn, and the issue remains open with no spec edit. KaspaCom, the one production implementer on record, calls its own deployed artifact "partially aligned, not fully conforming." Source: kccs repo . KCC-0021 and KCC-0402 are adopted standards already running in production Wrong Why not Both are open, unmerged pull requests. Neither is a merged spec. Their PR bodies claim production use (kascov, KaspaRocket, a k402 reference implementation on mainnet); those claims live inside the open proposals themselves and could not be independently confirmed. Source: kccs repo . Roadmap and app layer Claim Status Why DAGKnight is current mainnet consensus Research Where the branch stands No. Mainnet ordering runs GHOSTDAG. DAGKnight has a paper and a prototype branch. It is the consensus upgrade after Toccata. What it does not have is a merge: KIP-2 still reads Status: Proposed , even though the branch itself is active, with commits as recent as August 14, 2026 promoting its Universal Merge Consensus work. Source: KIP-2 raw file . vProgs have shipped as production app infrastructure Roadmap What the repo shows instead No. Zero releases, zero tags; the repo calls itself early development. Its tn10-flow example runs the flow against a private testnet-10 fork node, separate from the public one. A live Kaspa-native app layer needs its own shipped-product evidence. Source: vprogs repo . Argent proves Kaspa smart contracts are production-ready Research What the README claims is present No audit yet, and nothing has run on mainnet. Argent's own README says the main pieces are present: compiler, generated Silverscript, portable artifacts, runtime transaction building, multi-actor routing, and closed and open ICC. Silverscript has to finish its own audit first, then Argent needs hardening of its own. Source: Argent README . Native DeFi has shipped as a mature Kaspa L1 product layer Roadmap The covenant numbers behind that verdict Genuine early usage at small scale, with lending still absent from mainnet. Kaskad/Igra-style L2 lending is ecosystem context around Kaspa, separate from native L1 DeFi. See build-on-kaspa#covenant-adoption for current covenant counts and value; that figure moves fast enough that this page does not restate it. Testing a pitch built on top of Kaspa Five claim types, real vs. weak signal, and what other chains' product history says Use the claim fact-check above for protocol status, and the build page for a demo or txid used to prove a builder claim. Claim type Real signal Weak signal Kaspa question Launchpad Issuance, wallet flow, a liquidity path, visible holders, abuse controls. A token button and a roadmap. What can launch today, and where does the liquidity actually come from? DeFi Risk parameters, an oracle model, a liquidation path, an audit trail, liquidity, working transactions. The word "DeFi" stapled to any token page. Is this live mainnet, TN10/TN12 testnet evidence, or just an app idea riding on Toccata's name? AI agent The agent signs, pays, receives, proves work, or triggers a bounded workflow on-chain. Chatbot copy wrapped around a token. What action actually happens on Kaspa, and who can verify it? Wallet Clear signing, recovery, balances, history, error states, source verification. Nice screens with no real transaction handling underneath. Does a normal user know what they're signing? Institutional use Custody, compliance, reporting, settlement, liquidity, support, integration requirements. One vague partnership post. Which institution, which requirement, and what's the evidence? What other chains' product history says about the Kaspa gaps Observed behavior Consequence Kaspa gap Possible experiment Low-friction asset launches Creation, liquidity, and attention collapse into one flow. No Kaspa-native route from asset launch to tradable liquidity exists yet. A restrained post-Toccata asset tool with wallet safety, source labels, and abuse warnings. Swap aggregation Users want one route across liquidity sources instead of five tabs. No native DEX or swap routing yet. Track early swap attempts by quote quality, liquidity source, and signing UX. Hackathon intake Deadlines, judges, examples, and funding produce repeatable builder submissions. Builder activity here is less structured in public. A public Kaspa build sprint with source-backed judging criteria and shipped demos. Wallet-first apps Users judge a chain by signing, balances, errors, history, and support. Whitepapers do not enter into it. Consumer wallet UX is still fragmented across needs. Map wallet tasks from first user action to accepted transaction evidence. Exploit response Real DeFi needs monitoring, audits, an incident process, and recovery language before launch. Kaspa's app risk culture is still early. Require every app pitch to publish its failure modes before claiming production readiness. Both tables check whether a pitch names the parts a reviewer looks for. Neither says the product is worth building; that answer needs a named user and what they give up by switching. Code evidence Code and pull requests behind each track. A mainnet label still needs a release or activation record Track Recent public evidence How to read it Toccata / Silverscript TN12 dependency sync , KCC20 bootstrap fixes , and book/build fixes landed May 4-5, 2026. TN12 field testing surfaced developer-ergonomics issues around covenant and ZK opcode use. The v1.3.0-toc.5 pre-release sanity-tested mainnet pre-activation compatibility. The v2.0.0 release set the mainnet activation parameters; v2.0.1 followed as the Toccata release. The Toccata node setup guide adds operator guidance for upgrades, fee policy, API field changes, and Testnet-10 checks. The merged Rusty Kaspa ZK SDK PR adds an R0ScriptBuilder wrapper for turning RISC Zero receipts into Kaspa scripts, and the merged sequencing-lane PR adds the lane-proof plumbing that same script relies on. Both build on the public toccata branch . The earlier tn10-toc2 pre-release put Testnet-10 activation at DAA score 467,579,632; tn10-toc3 then scheduled final Toccata ZK hardening at DAA score 476,232,000, and a July 9 check of Testnet-10 REST status already read virtual DAA 512,574,907, past both scores. A July 25 recheck of the same endpoint showed virtual DAA 526,066,399, with 1,491,271 blocks. TN12 carried covenant opcode testing separately from TN10. Activated mainnet release evidence: release notes, activation parameters, the operator guide, TN10/TN12 testing, SDK and tooling prep. After activation, the next checks are wallets, explorers, examples, and accepted mainnet transactions. Toccata KIPs All four Toccata KIPs now read Status: Active in their raw files: KIP-16 (New Transaction Opcodes for Verifiable Computation), KIP-17 (Covenants and Improved Scripting Capabilities), KIP-20 (Covenant IDs), and KIP-21 (Partitioned Sequencing Commitment with O(activity) Proving). They moved together in commit e4ae2332 on July 15, 2026. Before that they were scoped to TN10, which is what makes the change worth recording: the spec repo caught up with the mainnet activation. The KIP status now matches the activation record instead of trailing it. Wallets, explorers, SDKs, and accepted mainnet transactions still carry their own separate evidence. Open KIP PRs KIP-24 is open for transaction version 1 fields and hashing; its draft text says v1 transactions add per-input compute budgets, optional output covenant bindings, user-lane subnetworks, and a BLAKE3 payload/rest txid split for ZK and based-executor workflows. KIP-25 is open for compute budget on script execution. KIP-22 is open for P2MR ScriptPublicKey, described as a Merkle-root pay-to-script form meant to hide public keys until spend time and support quantum-resistance and MAST-style conditional scripts. Worth knowing where the paperwork and the code disagree. Transaction version 1 and computeBudget already run on mainnet and are documented in the operator guide, but the KIPs that specify them, KIP-24 and KIP-25, are still open pull requests. Cite the guide or the node for those two. KIP-22 is separate: future cryptography and script-design work with no implementation behind it yet. Argent argent-lang/argent is an actor-based language and compiler for stateful, multi-contract applications on covenant-native UTXO rails. It compiles .ag source to plain Silverscript contracts and portable artifacts that argent-runtime turns into transactions: actors, state, transitions, named emits, and terminal become dispatch. It is where most of Michael Sutton's July output went, and it stayed active through July 31, adding Inter-Covenant Communication, actor enums, commitment-forest route planning, and a VS Code extension. Two sibling repos appeared: argent-playground on July 9 and argent-template on July 24. Examples now run well past the original Stones and Tickets. Compiler and runtime exist, gated on a Silverscript audit. No release, no crates.io publish. What the README claims The README calls the main pieces present: compiler, generated Silverscript, portable artifacts, runtime transaction building, multi-actor routing, and closed and open ICC. The gate it sets for itself is an audit. A production path opens once Silverscript completes its audit and is released, and Argent needs further audit and hardening after that. No release, no tag, no crates.io publish. Breaking-change commits on July 23 and 24 mean the ABI is still moving. A runtime transaction builder does exist now, argent-runtime 's TxBuilder and TxContext , which the README lists under what is useful today; what is still missing is generated app-specific builder APIs. The playground demos, including the DEX one, run fully offline against hardcoded fixtures with no node or RPC connection, so none of them is a deployment. vProgs The kaspanet/vprogs README describes an early-development Rust framework for based computation on Kaspa, with core, storage, state, scheduling, transaction-runtime, and node layers. A June 18 merge, Feat: Settlement into Covenants , gathered settlement-covenant work, transaction/batch/aggregation provers, SMT support, L1 bridge plumbing, and RISC Zero backend work into master, including a dedicated RISC0 backend commit . Roadmap implementation progress. Builders can study and experiment with the framework now. Production Kaspa app paths and native DeFi still need their own shipped evidence. See vProgs Explained . DAGKnight The public rusty-kaspa dagknight branch is active, most recently promoting Universal Merge Consensus work to the branch on August 14, 2026, on top of conflict-zone and lock-removal commits from August 13. Earlier branch history includes an encoding-test commit and a placeholder commit . Research and prototype evidence. Mainnet still runs GHOSTDAG; live finality and higher-BPS claims need their own activation evidence. Builder tooling kaspanet/kaspa-python-sdk is now a standalone public SDK repo. The v2.0.0 release added Toccata-aligned support and the full Rusty Kaspa managed-wallet API for Python. The v2.0.1 release adds get_seq_commit_lane_proof , SMT sync progress events, covenant-binding fixes, and a Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 dependency bump. Full detail sits in the changelog ; the package itself ships on PyPI . Developer-tooling progress that helps Python builders and integrators prepare for Toccata-era wallet, UTXO, lane-proof, and covenant workflows. Protocol-upgrade status still comes from node, KIP, and activation evidence. Infrastructure indexes rusty-kaspa PR #860 is open for review. It proposes an optional --txindex , a GetTransaction RPC path, inclusion and acceptance metadata, live updates from consensus notifications, resync from scratch, and pruning tied to retention-root changes. A separate relay draft PR explores a related path for propagating indexed data. Builder and infrastructure work that could help wallets, explorers, indexers, and large app-state workflows once merged. Operator checklist: who needs to check their path Ordinary wallet users have nothing to do; infrastructure operators each have a row. Ordinary users If you hold or send KAS from a normal wallet, there is nothing to do. Node upgrades are for people running infrastructure. Node operators Run Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 or newer. The node database upgrade only goes one way: the only path back is a resync. Wallets and submitters Use fee estimation, or update fixed-fee code to 100 sompi * max(compute grams, 2 * transaction bytes) . Before activation that floor bound only direct RPC submissions. The guide says relayed transactions are rejected under the same rule after activation, so it now binds both paths. Exchanges and indexers Update SDKs or regenerate bindings, then handle transaction version 1 , storageMass / storage_mass , computeBudget , output covenants, and UTXO covenant_id . Miners and pools Test block templates, job distribution, solved block reconstruction, and SubmitBlock against Testnet-10. A block that strips post-Toccata fields can turn invalid after the activation score. Pool accounting Check GetBlockRewardInfo , and GetSeqCommitLaneProof where lane-proof data matters. Infrastructure detail, but the kind that breaks payouts if skipped. Operator references: Toccata node setup guide and Go Kaspad v0.12.23 . A KCC is not a KIP Two numbered document series, two different jobs: what's decided, what's binding, what's adopted so far KIP KCC Decides Consensus and core-node behavior Conventions between independent implementations Binding on Every node that wants to stay on the network Whoever chooses to converge Adopted so far KIP-16, 17, 20, 21 active; KIP-2 still proposed KCC-0001, KCC-0002, and KCC-0020 merged, each still Status: Draft . None accepted. The kaspanet/kccs README draws the line itself: "KCCs do not propose changes to Kaspa consensus or core-node behavior... Acceptance marks an ecosystem convergence point; it does not make the convention protocol ground truth." See KIPs and KCCs for the live, per-proposal tracker; see the tokenomics table above for the KCC-0020 supply-split defect specifically. Common status questions DAGKnight: no, still research. Toccata: yes, activated. Smart contracts: L1 pieces live, vProgs still ahead Is DAGKnight live? No. DAGKnight is an adaptive consensus direction, still in research. Mainnet runs GHOSTDAG. The parameterless demo sets a latency assumption by hand and shows a fixed security parameter break where an adaptive one does not. Is Toccata live? Yes. Activation and adoption are separate questions. Check the table above before quoting wallet, explorer, or app state. Are Kaspa smart contracts live? Toccata put the L1 pieces live on mainnet: spend rules, asset rules, ZK proof checks, and sequencing commitments. A mature native app layer, with audited apps and broad tooling, is still ahead. Richer programmability through vProgs is later work. The shared state demo shows what Toccata already gives you against what vProgs would add. pages.title: Kaspa Risks and Open Questions | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: The strongest case against Kaspa, argued properly: what could go wrong and what would show it going wrong.
pages.text: What could go wrong Kaspa risks and open questions The case for Kaspa rests on a handful of separate claims, and any one of them can fail without the others failing. Seven risks, and what would settle each one Verification cost Higher block rates raise the bandwidth, CPU, and storage a node needs. Push that too far and only a few well-funded operators can still check the chain. What would settle it Many separate operators running nodes, APIs, explorers, and indexers. Fast blocks alone do not settle it. Security budget Block rewards decline over time. Unless fees and demand replace that revenue, miner income falls and so does the cost of attacking the network. What would settle it Fees and real demand paying for enough hash power over time. Price and enthusiasm alone do not settle it. Kaspa's block reward is 2.31246515 KAS (api.kaspa.org/info/blockreward): 864,000 blocks a day at 10 blocks per second, 1,997,970 KAS of new supply daily. At $0.02934513 per KAS (CoinGecko, read August 22, 2026), that's about $58,631 a day paid to miners, funding a network running at roughly 311.5 PH/s (api.kaspa.org/info/hashrate). Fees are a rounding error next to that: about 77,207 transactions a day at a median $0.000063 (this site's own chain data ) comes to $4.86 a day, roughly 1/12,054th of the subsidy, 0.0083%. The other 99.99% is new supply. Demand pays almost none of it. The subsidy is also shrinking on its own schedule. Kaspa's reward steps down every month by a factor of 2 −1/12 , about 5.61%, per rusty-kaspa's coinbase.rs subsidy table. Twelve of those steps compound to exactly half, so holding KAS price flat, the daily payout to miners falls to about $29,315 a year from now and about $3,664 in four years. Fees, unchanged, would need to grow about 6,000-fold in a year and 750-fold in four just to stay this far behind. That is the size of the gap they would have to close before catching up even starts. Catching up would take real transaction volume. Holding today's $0.000063 median fee flat, matching today's $58,631 subsidy from fees alone needs about 10,771 transactions per second, held continuously. A momentary peak would not be enough. That's roughly 12,000 times Kaspa's own 0.894 tx/s on the same 22 Aug 2026 one-day snapshot this section's other figures use (77,207 daily transactions divided by 86,400 seconds, per CLAIMS.yml 's fees_vs_subsidy_2026_08_22 entry), and higher than any one-day sustained rate in this site's own comparison data, including Solana's 1,579.6 on that same one-day basis (see the mining page's traffic-scenarios sourcing for the full derivation; the site's 30-day means, a different and larger figure for a bursty chain like Kaspa, are on chain-comparer ). Holding today's transaction count flat instead, the same match needs a median fee near $0.76, about six times Bitcoin's own $0.1317 median. Neither looks close, and both would have to happen while the subsidy itself keeps shrinking underneath them. This isn't unique to Kaspa: Bitcoin has run the same subsidy-funded deficit for its entire existence and remains the hardest chain to attack. Today, Kaspa's security is bought almost entirely with inflation. People paying to use the chain fund almost none of it, and no visible trend closes that gap on fees alone. The attack cost calculator prices what it costs to outrun this hash rate for an hour. External cost PoW security is bought with power, ASICs, and supply chains. That cost is real, and a fast chain does not make it go away. Liquidity Depth, custody, exchange support, and market makers do not follow from good design. They take years and money. What would settle it Users able to get in and out, hold their own keys, keep books, get help, and trade at depth. Holders and volume existing on their own do not settle it. Mining concentration A small number of makers control ASIC Application-specific integrated circuit: a chip built to do one job, in Kaspa's case running kHeavyHash, fast. It cannot be reprogrammed for anything else the way a general-purpose CPU or GPU can. supply. Pools cluster, and so does geography, so control can land in few hands even with an open protocol. Fair-launch context No premine does not mean no early concentration. The fair-launch comparison plots Kaspa's genesis supply against Ethereum, Cardano, and XRP, and what a fair launch does and doesn't guarantee. Roadmap execution Toccata activated on mainnet. vProgs, DAGKnight, and native DeFi are still separate tracks on separate timelines; a testnet demo of one is not evidence for the rest. What would settle it A mainnet release and proof it turned on, with wallets, indexers, accepted transactions, and repeat flows. A talk, a branch, or a testnet demo does not settle it. Risk What would answer it? Toccata tooling stays rough after it turns on. Toccata activated at DAA score 474,165,565, the score set by Rusty Kaspa v2.0.0, with v2.0.1 released after it. What's left to check Stable releases, docs that work, and builder examples anyone can repeat. TN10 A Kaspa test network used to trial protocol changes, including Toccata, ahead of mainnet activation. / TN12 A separate Kaspa test network used to trial covenant and script changes ahead of mainnet. tests alone are not enough. Native apps stay demos with no users. Repeat users, real fee demand, wallets, separate indexers, and apps that keep working. DeFi claims get ahead of custody and oracles. Audited custody rules and real wallet signing. An oracle design, liquidation rules, and settlement that gets accepted. Based-app language becomes too abstract. Real products where app state is tied to Kaspa ordering, proofs, settlement, or exits. User demand Low fees and spare room are needed for apps to exist. They are no proof that anyone will use them twice. What would settle it People coming back because an app does the job better on Kaspa than on a normal server. Low fees alone do not settle it. Try it Price the security budget yourself The security-budget risk above turns on one number: what it costs to outrun Kaspa's hash rate. Run the attack-cost calculator on the mining page and set your own time window to see that cost priced live. What to watch How many separate node, API, and indexer operators exist. Whether roadmap items turn into apps with repeat users. Staying a demo does not count. And how fast the words live, testnet, roadmap, and research get flattened into one story in a hype cycle. For the price and hash-rate version, read Kaspa price, hash rate, and the mining cycle . Keep reading Next pages Previous Kaspa current status What is live, targeted, roadmap, and research on Kaspa right now, checked against mainnet, releases, and KIPs. pages.title: Kaspa Mining | Kaspa Explained
pages.description: Why Kaspa price and hash rate move on different clocks, and how to point your own ASIC at your own node.
pages.text: Proof-of-work mining Kaspa mining Price can fall while hash rate climbs. A coin market reprices in minutes; a machine market (ASIC orders, shipping, hosting, wiring) answers weeks or months later. Checked August 22, 2026: Toccata activated at DAA score Difficulty-Adjusted Age: a running block count Kaspa consensus uses instead of wall-clock time, since many blocks land in parallel. 474,165,565; Rusty Kaspa v2.0.1 is the release. Not a price call. Snapshot Checked August 22, 2026 KAS price CoinGecko: $0.02926 per KAS on August 22, 2026, up from $0.0269 on August 8. Coinbase all-time high: $0.2075 . A status snapshot, not a price call. Network hash rate Kaspa API: 312.1 PH/s , up from 282.4 PH/s on August 8. Kaspa wiki: 500 TH/s on November 29, 2022. i Why compare to the 500 TH/s milestone Rough comparison: 312 PH/s is about 624 times the wiki's 500 TH/s milestone from November 2022. These numbers move by the week. Supply Kaspa API: 27.655B KAS circulating of 28.704B KAS maximum supply. Block reward Kaspa API: 2.31246515 KAS per block, the emission step beginning at DAA score 504,909,000 (10 BPS era), unchanged since August 8. The two markets The cycle What to watch Solo mining setup Sources The two markets A proof-of-work coin runs two markets on two clocks: one reprices in minutes, the other answers months later. Clocks Full loop Coin market minutes to days price, liquidity, sentiment Machine market weeks to months ASIC orders, shipping, hosting, hash rate, difficulty Hash rate can fall and still sit far above where it was a year ago. Used ASIC prices can collapse after new production overshoots demand that already cooled. Miners chase margin. Holders chase an exit or hold through it. Buyers chase a price they can stomach. ASIC makers chase order volume. The snapshot above holds both at once, a price downtrend and a multi-year hash-rate buildout. Coin demand Moves first Demand, liquidity, attention, and holder behavior reprice KAS within hours. Miner revenue Sets the day's math Price, block reward, fees, difficulty, and power cost decide whether mining pays that day. ASIC demand Capital follows margin Profitable mining pulls capital toward hardware orders and hosting contracts. Hash rate Arrives late ASICs ordered on a price signal can come online after that signal has already faded. Difficulty Compresses margin More machines compete for the same block reward, so each machine earns less KAS per unit of hash rate. Used machines Sort the survivors The cold phase moves hardware, coins, and conviction to whoever can outlast it. Visual shelf: market lag and miner margin Price and hash rate Divergence here is the lag working as expected, not a contradiction. Miner margin Price, block reward, fees, difficulty, hardware cost, and electricity price all land on the same miner at once. Cycle model Coins and ASICs heat and cool at different times This framing is an outside opinion, not a sourced protocol fact: an X account, @Themooseisloos5, cast the coin-and-ASIC cycle as a Carnot-engine model, four phases, borrowing the thermodynamics term for an engine that cycles between a hot and a cold state. Four phases The hot/cold cycle and Kaspa's compressed history Phase-by-phase breakdown of coin and ASIC market timing. 1 Hot coins, cold ASICs Demand moves into KAS before hardware can respond. Price rises, mining margins expand, and idle or cheap machines suddenly pencil out. 2 Hot coins, hot ASICs ASIC demand catches up. New machines get ordered, old machines get repriced upward, hash rate climbs, and early holders or miners start taking profit. 3 Cold coins, hot ASICs Price cools while machines already on order keep arriving. Difficulty can rise into a weak market, which crushes miner margins further. 4 Cold coins, cold ASICs Weak miners shut off or sell. Used machines get cheaper. Coins consolidate. The system compresses until demand, hardware, and conviction find a new balance. Kaspa compressed into one short window several discovery phases that took Bitcoin years: fair launch, fast emissions, GPU mining, an ASIC transition, exchange discovery, and price discovery all landed close together, followed by a large mining buildout. Bitcoin's early distribution, hardware maturation, exchange access, and public understanding all spread out over a much longer stretch. Compression cuts both ways. A bigger up and a bigger down both become more likely, and whether that produces a stronger base is not visible in real time. It shows up one, two, five years later, if it shows up at all. Proof of work distributes coins through hardware, electricity, and time instead of a capital-first allocation, and miners still have to cover their costs. Kaspa's fast emission schedule moves supply toward its cap quickly, which is part of the hard-money thesis. The same speed front-loads distribution pressure. Early miners earned coins by running hardware, with no allocation sold up front. That's the fair-launch case. It also means the early market absorbs a steady flow of coins moving from early miners and holders into later buyers: some take profit, some miners sell to cover power and hardware bills, some holders panic, some accumulate. Fair distribution on paper can still produce an ugly chart. Conviction usually gets tested on the downside. The upside tests it too, since rallies tempt profit-taking the same way drawdowns tempt capitulation. How this works, and the sources Kaspa's reward drops by about 5.61% (a factor of 2 to the power of −1/12) roughly every month, forever, on a schedule fixed in the software from day one. There is no single "halving day": every step is the same small size as the one before it, and the trigger is a block counter internal to the network, not the calendar. The counter is called DAA score, the network's own clock. For roughly the first six months after mainnet (Nov 2021), the reward held flat at 500 KAS per block, a bootstrap period, not part of the halving schedule. Verified in rusty-kaspa's consensus/core/src/config/params.rs : pre_deflationary_phase_base_subsidy is 500 KAS, active until deflationary_phase_daa_score 15,519,600. After that, the monthly-halving schedule took over, starting at 440 KAS per block-second, per the SUBSIDY_BY_MONTH_TABLE in consensus/src/processes/coinbase.rs . On 5 May 2025, the Crescendo hard fork moved Kaspa from 1 block per second to 10 (DAA score 110,165,000, per the v1.0.0 release notes). That split the same monthly reward across ten times as many blocks; it did not change how much is issued per month. That's why a reward chart drawn before and after Crescendo looks continuous instead of jumping. The reward right now, the total mined to date, and Kaspa's maximum supply all come from a live read of api.kaspa.org/info/blockdag and api.kaspa.org/info/coinsupply . Signal Too-fast reading Slower reading Price down The market lost interest. Lost demand, miner selling, early-holder profit-taking, broad market weakness, and leverage unwinds can all produce the same line, separately or together. Hash rate down The network is failing. Go deeper: linear charts hide the thing people actually care about A linear chart makes the dollar swing dominate the page. A log chart shows the percentage change a holder actually feels. A move from $10 to $20 and a move from $10,000 to $20,000 are both 2x. The dollar amounts feel wildly different. The percentage effect on a holder's position is identical. Log scale fits a young network better than linear. An 80% drawdown looks like death on a linear chart. On a log chart, the same drawdown can read as one violent move inside a much longer compounding path. The eye tracks distance on the page. The portfolio tracks percentage change. Drawdowns are still real losses for whoever is holding them. A top buyer sees a straight loss. An early holder may be looking at a brutal drawdown measured from absurd gains. Someone who bought early and never sold can be living through both pain and life-changing profit in the same chart. Go deeper: market cap is not a pile of cash Market cap marks the whole supply at the last trade. Active float and buyer depth decide how easily that price moves. Market cap is total supply marked at the marginal price. It isn't a pool of cash sitting somewhere. A 20% price drop does not mean sellers extracted 20% of the market cap in cash. A small amount of selling can move price a long way once buyers step back. A liquidation can dump coins into market inventory that takes the market weeks or months to absorb. Sellers can keep leaning on the order book because they need liquidity before they need conviction. Market cap looks like a pool of money. Price is set at the edge, where the next buyer meets the next seller. Active float sets selloff pressure: how many coins are actually for sale, how urgent those sellers are, and how deep the buyers sit at each price rung. Total supply matters for the monetary story. Float matters in a selloff. A large liquidation keeps reshaping the market long after the candle closes, as coins move from one kind of holder into another kind of inventory. The wallet-level story needs stronger sourcing before naming actors. Go deeper: miners do not get to be pure believers A miner can believe in the network and still sell. Hardware, hosting, power, repairs, taxes, and debt create pressure a holder never faces. A holder can decide to sit still. A miner has bills: electricity, hosting, hardware debt, repairs, taxes, pool fees, upgrades. Thin margins turn a believer into a seller regardless of conviction. Mining paid well when price outran hash rate, and ASICs got expensive because that revenue opportunity was real: some machines ran tens of thousands of dollars during the hot phase. Operators with that cost basis recoup it partly by selling coins. Evidence Fees are the second revenue source Issuance pays miners first; fees have to matter later, the open security-budget question. Whether Kaspa is healthy or failing on that question is not knowable in real time. How the mempool actually picks, not sorts rusty-kaspa's mempool does not keep a strictly sorted fee queue. Its Frontier weighs each candidate transaction by feerate^alpha with alpha = 3 , where feerate is fee divided by mass, in sompi per gram. When total pending mass fits in one block it takes everything (no sampling needed, matching the "every transaction fits" state below). When it doesn't, it draws a weighted random sample rather than a strict ranking, so a lower-fee transaction can get pulled in and a higher-fee one can still be waiting after the draw. Transactions are also grouped into lanes by subnetwork, and once enough lanes are represented, lane assignment freezes and selection continues within those lanes; this demo does not model lanes, only the feerate-weighted sampling itself. This demo's own "picked vs. waiting" simulation approximates that principle (weighted-random draw, not the literal k·log(n) sampling algorithm or lane logic) using an illustrative, not measured, spread of other transactions' fees, since Kaspa's blocks carry too little real traffic today to have an observed fee distribution to draw from. weight(tx) = feerate(tx)^3 feerate = fee_sompi / mass_grams Source: mining/src/mempool/model/frontier.rs and mining/src/feerate/mod.rs .
